description: Clean Code, SOLID and all 23 Gang of Four (GoF) design patterns, plus the patterns and ideas that came after (Fowler, Kerievsky, Bloch, Nystrom, Wlaschin), each rooted in concrete scenarios: which pattern for this situation, which smell calls for it, and when not to use it.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Code review: int d; // elapsed time in days. What does Clean Code ask you to do, and why?
notes.back: Rename it, e.g. elapsedTimeInDays, and delete the comment. The name should carry the intent everywhere d is used; the comment only helps on this one line.
notes.analogy: A labelled jar beats an unlabelled jar with a sticky note that falls off when you move it.
notes.extra: Rule: if a name needs a comment, the name does not reveal its intent.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Why is i fine as a loop counter in a 3-line loop but bad as a class field?
notes.back: Name length should match scope size. In a tiny scope the context explains i; a field is read far from its declaration and needs a descriptive, searchable name.
notes.extra: Reverse for functions: widely used public methods can have short names (open()); private helpers with narrow scope can afford long, precise names.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Why does Clean Code reject strName, m_count and IShapeFactory?
notes.back: They encode type or scope into the name. Modern editors and type systems show that, and encodings go stale when the type changes.
notes.extra: Interface case: Martin prefers the plain ShapeFactory for the interface and marks the implementation (ShapeFactoryImpl) if one must be marked.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Clean Code: when should you pick a solution-domain name (JobQueue, AccountVisitor) vs a problem-domain name (Policy, Claim)?
notes.back: Use computer science terms for technical machinery: readers are programmers. Use the business's vocabulary for domain concepts, so the code can be checked against what experts say.
notes.extra: Smell: a Claim called RecordHolder hides the domain; a hand-rolled queue called WaitingClaims hides that it is just a queue.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Why does Clean Code say not to pun, e.g. using add() both for summing two values and for inserting into a collection?
notes.back: One word, one meaning. Readers who know add as "combine values" will misuse an add that inserts. Call it insert or append.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: A renderPage() calls getHtml(), then does buf.append("\n"), then includeSetupPages(). Which function rule does it break?
notes.back: One level of abstraction per function: high-level steps are mixed with low-level string fiddling, so readers can't tell essential steps from detail.
notes.analogy: A recipe that says "make the sauce", then "turn the knob 37° clockwise", then "bake the lasagne".
notes.extra: Fix: push the append into a well-named helper so every line reads at the same level.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: What is Clean Code's stepdown rule?
notes.back: Code reads top-down: each function is followed by the next-level functions it calls, so the file reads like "To do X, we do Y and Z" paragraphs.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Clean Code: how can you test whether a function does "one thing"?
notes.back: Try to extract another function from it whose name is not just a restatement of its implementation. If you can, it was doing more than one thing.
notes.extra: Also: visible sections inside a function ("// declarations", "// initialisation", "// sieve") are a sign it does several things.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: calculatePay(e), isPayday(e) and deliverPay(e) each switch on e.type. What does Clean Code prescribe?
notes.back: Tolerate the switch once: bury it in the code that creates the right Employee subtype, and let polymorphism handle every operation afterwards.
notes.extra: Why: repeated switches on the same type code must all be found and edited when a new employee type arrives.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Why does Clean Code rank function arguments niladic > monadic > dyadic, and treat three or more as needing special justification?
notes.back: Each argument is a concept the reader must hold in mind, and test cases multiply with argument combinations. Dyads with no natural order invite swaps.
notes.extra: Example: assertEquals(expected, actual): people swap the two all the time, because nothing in the call says which is which.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Is makeCircle(Point center, double radius) instead of makeCircle(double x, double y, double radius) just cheating on argument count?
notes.back: No. x and y always travel together: they are one concept, and an argument object gives that concept a name and a home for its behaviour.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Code review: render(true). What is wrong and what is the fix?
notes.back: A flag argument announces that the function does two things, and the call site can't tell which. Split it: renderForSuite() and renderForSingleTest().
notes.analogy: A light switch labelled only "true": you have to read the wiring to know what it does.
notes.extra: Milder fix: where splitting is awkward, a named enum (render(Mode.SUITE)) at least makes the call readable.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Why does Clean Code dislike output arguments, as in appendFooter(report)?
notes.back: Readers expect arguments to be inputs, so they must check the signature to learn that report is mutated. In OO, prefer report.appendFooter(): the object being changed is the receiver.
notes.analogy: Handing a form to a clerk and getting it back with your answers changed: you only expect them to read it.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: checkPassword(user, pw) also calls Session.initialize() when the password matches. What is the problem?
notes.back: A hidden side effect: the name promises a check only. It creates temporal coupling: calling it at the wrong time silently wipes a session.
notes.analogy: A doorbell that also unlocks the back door: pressing it to check if anyone is home has consequences.
notes.extra: Fix: separate the two, or at least be honest: checkPasswordAndInitializeSession (which also reveals it does two things).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: if (set("username", "bob")) …: which principle does set violate, and how do you fix it?
notes.back: Command-query separation (CQS): a function should either change state or answer a question, not both. Here the reader can't tell if it asks "was it set?" or "did it exist?".
notes.analogy: A question that is also an order: "Is the oven on?" that switches it on.
notes.extra:
if (attributeExists("username")) {
  setAttribute("username", "bob");
}

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Command-query separation (CQS): where is breaking it the right call?
notes.back: When the operation must be atomic: stack.pop(), queue.poll(), map.putIfAbsent(), compare-and-set. Splitting query and command opens a race between them.
notes.extra: Contrast: in single-threaded domain code, the split costs nothing and removes ambiguity, so keep CQS there.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Clean Code says the body of an if or while should usually be one line. What does that line tend to be, and why?
notes.back: A call to a well-named function. The name documents the branch, and the indentation never goes beyond one or two levels.
notes.extra:
if (isTestPage(pageData))
  includeSetupAndTeardownPages(pageData, isSuite);

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Does Clean Code require Dijkstra's single entry / single exit (no early return, no break)?
notes.back: Not for small functions: an early return or guard clause there is clearer than nested flags. The rule pays off only in large functions, which you shouldn't have anyway.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Clean Code's own refactorings split a method into tiny methods that share data through instance fields. What is the critique, beyond fragmentation?
notes.back: Arguments become hidden mutable state: each tiny method reads and writes fields, so order matters and its inputs are invisible. That reintroduces hidden side effects.
notes.extra: Better: extract functions that take inputs and return results; promote to fields only when a cohesive new class emerges.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: What is the Boy Scout Rule, and what is a concrete example of it?
notes.back: Leave the code a little cleaner than you found it. While fixing a bug in invoice.ts, rename one cryptic variable or extract one tangled condition.
notes.analogy: Leave the campsite cleaner than you found it: nobody cleans the whole forest, yet it never gets worse.
notes.extra: Limit: keep the clean-up small and, ideally, in its own commit, so a bug-fix review doesn't turn into a rewrite review.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.text: Clean Code's acceptable comments: {{c1::legal}} (copyright header); {{c2::intent}} (why this choice); {{c3::warning of consequences}} ("takes 40 min to run"); {{c4::TODO}}; {{c5::public API documentation}}.
notes.extra: Common thread: each says something the code cannot: rationale, risk, or the contract for callers who never see the code.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front:
Rewrite this in Clean Code style:
// eligible for full benefits?
if ((e.flags & HOURLY) && e.age > 65)
notes.back: if (employee.isEligibleForFullBenefits()). Explain yourself in code: move the knowledge into a named method, and the comment becomes redundant.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Which kind of comment is // Not thread-safe: SimpleDateFormat is shared; create one per call, and is it acceptable?
notes.back: A warning of consequences. Acceptable: it tells the next editor about a danger they cannot see in the code.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: A file starts with 40 lines of // 2019-03-02 JD: fixed rounding entries. What does Clean Code say?
notes.back: Delete these journal comments. Version control records who changed what and when, and that log never drifts from the code.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Why is commented-out code especially harmful?
notes.back: Nobody dares delete it ("it must be there for a reason"), so it piles up and rots, yet it never runs or gets tested. Delete it: git remembers.
notes.analogy: Boxes in the attic labelled "maybe important": nobody opens them, nobody throws them away.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Your linter forces a doc comment on every method, so you get @param name the name. Why is that worse than nothing?
notes.back: Mandated, redundant comments add noise that trains readers to skip comments, including the rare ones that matter, and they go stale.
notes.extra: Keep doc comments for public APIs where they state contract, units and edge cases.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: A function ends with } // while and } // try. What does the comment tell you?
notes.back: The function is too long: you need markers to match braces. Shorten it instead of labelling its closing braces.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: When is a // TODO acceptable in Clean Code, and what keeps it honest?
notes.back: When it records work that can't be done now (waiting on an API, a known limitation). Scan and clean TODOs regularly; it is no excuse to leave bad code.
notes.extra: In practice: link the TODO to a ticket, so it lives in a backlog, not only in the source.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: What is Clean Code's newspaper metaphor for a source file?
notes.back: The name is the headline; the top gives the high-level concepts and algorithms; detail increases as you read down, so readers can stop once they have enough.
notes.analogy: A news article: headline, then a summary paragraph, then ever finer detail for those who keep reading.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Clean Code formatting: what should blank lines and their absence signal?
notes.back: Blank lines separate concepts (vertical openness); lines that belong together stay dense, with no comment or blank line breaking them apart.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::01 Clean Code: Names, Functions & Comments
notes.front: Clean Code's vertical distance rules for where to place a variable and a called function?
notes.back: Declare local variables close to their first use. Put a caller above its callee and near it, so the reader scrolls down, not around.
notes.extra: Conceptual affinity: functions that do similar things (overloads, assertTrue / assertFalse) sit together even if they don't call each other.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Object vs data structure, in Clean Code's sense?
notes.back: An object hides its data and exposes behaviour. A data structure exposes its data and has no meaningful behaviour.
notes.extra: Point: getters and setters for every field don't make an object; they make a data structure with extra steps.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: You have Square, Circle, Triangle and need to add perimeter(). Which design makes that cheap: procedural Geometry.area(shape) with a switch, or polymorphic shape.area()?
notes.back: Procedural: write one new function; the shape structs don't change. In the OO version every shape class must gain a method.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Same shapes, but now you must add Hexagon. Which design makes that cheap?
notes.back: Object-oriented: add one class, and existing code is untouched. In the procedural version every function's switch must learn about hexagons.
notes.extra: Rule: choose by what you expect to grow, operations or types. This trade-off is known as the expression problem.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: When does Clean Code say procedural code over plain data structures beats objects?
notes.back: When the set of types is stable and new operations keep arriving: a compiler's syntax tree with many passes, or a report pipeline over fixed DTOs.
notes.extra: Martin: "Mature programmers know that the idea that everything is an object is a myth."

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: An Order has public setters for every field and also calculateTotal(), while callers compute totals themselves too. What does Clean Code call this, and why is it bad?
notes.back: A hybrid: half object, half data structure. It is hard to add new functions and hard to add new types, so it gets the worst of both.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: ctxt.getOptions().getScratchDir().getAbsolutePath(): when is this a Law of Demeter violation, and when not?
notes.back: A violation if those are objects (their internals should be hidden). If they are plain data structures exposing data by design, the law does not apply.
notes.extra: Note: storing each step in a local variable doesn't fix a real violation; the caller still knows the whole structure.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: You need ctxt.getOptions().getScratchDir().getAbsolutePath() to create a temp file. What is the Clean Code fix?
notes.back: Ask why you need the path, then tell the object to do that: ctxt.createScratchFileStream(name). The context hides where its scratch dir lives.
notes.analogy: Instead of asking the hotel for the key to the store room, you ask reception for a towel.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Data transfer object (DTO): what is it and where does it belong?
notes.back: A class with public data and no behaviour, used to move data across a boundary: database rows, network messages, API payloads. Keep business rules out of it.
notes.extra: Martin on Active Record: treat the record as a data structure and put business rules in separate objects that hold it.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.back: Error return codes force each caller to check immediately, nesting the happy path inside error checks. Exceptions let the happy path read straight through, with handling in one place.
notes.extra: Bonus: a shared Error enum becomes a dependency magnet: adding a code recompiles every user.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Clean Code's rule "error handling is one thing": what should a function containing try look like?
notes.back: try is the first word and nothing follows the catch/finally. The try body is one call, e.g. deletePageAndAllReferences(page), and the catch calls logError(e).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Why does Clean Code argue that checked exceptions (Java's throws clauses) violate the open/closed principle?
notes.back: A new checked exception thrown at the lowest level forces every signature up the call chain to change, even in modules that don't care. Encapsulation breaks along the path.
notes.extra: Context: C#, Kotlin, Python and TypeScript have no checked exceptions; Java's own newer APIs largely avoid them.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: A third-party ACMEPort throws DeviceResponseException, ATM1212UnlockedException and GMXError, and your callers handle all three identically. What does Clean Code suggest?
notes.back: Wrap the API in your own LocalPort that translates them into one PortDeviceFailure. Define exception classes by how callers catch them, not by their source.
notes.analogy: A travel adapter: every foreign socket shape converted into the one plug your devices know.
notes.extra: Bonus: the wrapper is also the single place to swap vendors or fake the port in tests.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Clean Code: what should an exception message contain?
notes.back: Enough context to locate the failure: the operation that was attempted and the kind of failure, e.g. "loading invoice 42: file not found", not just "error".

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.back: An exception drives a normal business case. Have the data access object (DAO) return a special-case object whose total is the per-diem, so the caller needs no branch.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: List<Employee> getEmployees() returns null when there are none. What breaks and what is the fix?
notes.back: Every caller must remember a null check; one forgotten check is a NullPointerException far from the cause. Return an empty list so loops just do nothing.
notes.analogy: An empty mailbox is still a mailbox; a missing mailbox makes the postman crash into the lawn.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Why is passing null (calc.xProjection(null, p2)) worse than returning it?
notes.back: The callee has no good response: throw, assert, or guess. Most callers never meant to pass it. Clean Code's default: forbid null arguments, and make the type system enforce it.
notes.extra: Modern: TypeScript strictNullChecks, Kotlin String? and C# nullable reference types turn "don't pass null" into a compile error.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Java Optional<T> vs null: where is Optional meant to be used?
notes.back: As a return type for "maybe absent", so the caller must decide. Not as a field or parameter type, and never for collections (return an empty one).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: A Map<String, Sensor> is passed through dozens of methods. Why does Clean Code suggest wrapping it in a Sensors class?
notes.back: The raw Map exposes too much (clear(), any key) and spreads the third-party interface everywhere. Sensors.getById(id) exposes only what you need and confines changes to one class.
notes.extra: Rule: keep boundary interfaces inside the class or close family that uses them; don't return them from public APIs.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: What is a learning test, and what is its long-term payoff?
notes.back: A unit test you write against a third-party API to learn how it behaves. Keep them: when you upgrade the library, they tell you at once if its behaviour changed.
notes.analogy: Testing the ice with a stick before you walk on it, and again every winter.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: You must call a radio API that another team hasn't designed yet. What does Clean Code suggest?
notes.back: Define the interface you wish you had (e.g. Transmitter.transmit(freq, stream)), code against it now, and write a thin adapter once the real API exists.
notes.extra: Bonus: your interface also gives you a seam for a fake in tests.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Why does Clean Code say test code is as important as production code?
notes.back: Dirty tests get harder to change than the code, so the team eventually deletes them. Without tests, people fear changing code, and the production code rots.
notes.analogy: Scaffolding nobody maintains: once it rusts, workers stop climbing it, and repairs to the building stop.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: A test has 40 lines of fixture-building noise before one assertion. What does Clean Code recommend?
notes.back: Build a small domain-specific testing language: helpers like makePages("PageOne", "PageOne.ChildOne") and assertResponseContains(...), so each test reads build, operate, check.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: "One assert per test" vs "one concept per test": which does Clean Code endorse?
notes.back: One concept per test. Several asserts are fine if they check one behaviour; testing "add a month to a 31-day month" and "to a 30-day month" belongs in two tests.
notes.extra: Why: a failing test name should tell you which behaviour broke.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Clean Code's dual standard for test code?
notes.back: Tests must be just as clean and readable as production code, but needn't be as efficient: a slow string concatenation or extra allocation is fine in a test.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: testUpdateUser passes when run alone but fails after testCreateUser. Which F.I.R.S.T. property is broken (Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely), and what is the fix?
notes.back: Independent: the tests share state, e.g. a database row or a static. Give each test its own setup and clean-up.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: A unit test calls the real payment sandbox and fails whenever the network is slow. Which F.I.R.S.T. properties (Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely) does it break?
notes.back: Fast and Repeatable: it depends on an environment you don't control. Put the sandbox behind your own interface and use a fake in unit tests.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.text: Martin's three laws of test-driven development (TDD): (1) write no production code until you have {{c1::a failing unit test}}; (2) write no more of a test than is {{c2::sufficient to fail}} (not compiling counts as failing); (3) write no more production code than is {{c3::sufficient to pass the current failing test}}.
notes.extra: Effect: a cycle of tens of seconds, so you are never more than a minute from green.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Main critique of Martin's three laws of test-driven development (TDD) taken literally?
notes.back: Such tiny steps encourage tests that mirror implementation steps rather than behaviour, and leave little room to think about design up front.
notes.extra: Middle path: Beck himself varies step size: tiny when unsure, larger when confident.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Why is "passes all the tests" the first rule of simple design, and what does it do to design?
notes.back: A design you can't verify is worthless. Making code testable also pushes it towards small, decoupled classes with injected dependencies.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Simple design: class FullName wraps a single string used in two places. Under the "fewest elements" rule, should you inline it?
notes.back: Only if it adds nothing. If it carries intent or validation, "reveals intention" outranks "fewest elements", so keep it. Delete classes that exist only for speculative structure.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: Clean Code measures class size by responsibilities, not lines. What quick test does it give?
notes.back: Describe the class in about 25 words without "if", "and", "or" or "but". Vague names like Manager, Processor or Super also hint at too many responsibilities.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: ReportGenerator has fields pdfFont and margins used only by renderPdf(), and smtpHost used only by email(). What does that tell you?
notes.back: Low cohesion: methods split into clusters that use disjoint fields. Each cluster wants to be its own class, e.g. PdfRenderer and ReportMailer.
notes.extra: Ideal: each method uses most of the class's fields.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::02 Clean Code: Objects, Errors, Boundaries & Tests
notes.front: You extract a helper from a big function, and it needs four of the function's locals. Clean Code's move, and where it leads?
notes.back: Promote the locals to fields so the helper takes no arguments. Cohesion then drops, which shows a new class waiting to be split out. Many small classes emerge.
notes.extra: Watch: stop before the fields become hidden shared state between methods (see the tiny-functions critique).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Single responsibility principle (SRP): what does "responsibility" mean, precisely?
notes.back: A reason to change, which Martin ties to one actor: one group of people who request changes. A module should answer to one actor.
notes.extra: Not: "does one thing"; that rule is for functions.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Employee has calculatePay() (for accounting), reportHours() (for HR) and save() (for the DBAs). Both use a shared regularHours(). What goes wrong?
notes.back: Accounting asks to change overtime rules; a developer edits regularHours(); HR's reports silently become wrong. Three actors are coupled through one class.
notes.analogy: One shared spreadsheet tab used by accounting and HR: accounting edits a formula and HR's numbers quietly change.
notes.extra: Fix: separate PayCalculator, HourReporter, EmployeeRepository over a plain EmployeeData.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: OrderService.process() validates input, prices the order, saves it and sends the confirmation email. How do you apply the single responsibility principle (SRP)?
notes.back: Spot the separate reasons to change (validation rules, pricing, storage, messaging) and give each its own class; process() becomes a short orchestrator calling them.
notes.analogy: A restaurant where the chef also takes orders, washes dishes and does the books: any one job changing disrupts the others.
notes.extra:
void process(Order o) {
  validator.check(o);
  o.setTotal(pricing.priceOf(o));
  repo.save(o);
  notifier.confirm(o); }

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: When is splitting by the single responsibility principle (SRP) overkill?
notes.back: When the "responsibilities" always change together and for the same person, as in a small script or a thin CRUD endpoint. Split when change history shows them diverging.
notes.extra: Cost of over-splitting: five classes and four interfaces for 40 lines of logic; readers must jump through files to follow one request.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Single responsibility principle (SRP) vs "a function should do one thing": how to tell them apart?
notes.back: SRP: modules, and who causes change (actors). "Do one thing": a function's level of abstraction. A class of many single-purpose functions can still serve one actor.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Open/closed principle (OCP): what does "open for extension, closed for modification" mean in practice?
notes.back: You can add new behaviour by adding code (a new class, a new function, a new config entry) without editing code that already works and is tested.
notes.analogy: A power strip: plug in a new appliance without rewiring the house.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: DiscountCalculator has if (tier == "GOLD") … else if (tier == "SILVER") … and you edit it for every new tier. Which principle, and the fix?
notes.back: Open/closed principle (OCP). Introduce an extension point: a DiscountPolicy interface (or a map from tier to function) chosen once; a new tier is a new entry.
notes.extra:
interface DiscountPolicy { Money apply(Order o); }
Map<Tier, DiscountPolicy> policies = ...;
policies.get(c.tier()).apply(order);

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Open/closed principle (OCP): name three extension points that need no class hierarchy.
notes.back: A function parameter (sortBy(keyFn)), a data table / config (tax rates per country), and a plugin or hook registry (handlers registered by name).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Why can't code be closed against every kind of change, and how do you pick?
notes.back: Each extension point costs indirection and only covers the axis you guessed. Close against the changes you have actually seen: take the first hit, then add the extension point.
notes.extra: Martin: "strategic closure". Also called "fool me once".

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Open/closed principle (OCP) vs YAGNI (you aren't gonna need it): how do they fit together?
notes.back: OCP says build extension points; YAGNI says don't build for imagined needs. Together: hard-code the first variant, and add the extension point when a real second variant arrives.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Liskov substitution principle (LSP): what does it require?
notes.back: Code written against a base type must keep working with any subtype, without knowing which it got. Subtypes must honour the base type's behavioural contract, not just its signatures.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Square extends Rectangle. Why does r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); assert r.area() == 20 fail with a square, and what principle breaks?
notes.back: Square.setHeight also changes the width, so area is 16. Rectangle promised that setting height leaves width alone: Liskov substitution breaks.
notes.extra: Fixes: make shapes immutable (withWidth() returns a new shape), or don't relate them by inheritance.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Why is "is-a in the real world" the wrong test for inheritance, per Liskov?
notes.back: What matters is behaviour callers rely on. A square is a rectangle in geometry, but a mutable Square can't keep a mutable Rectangle's promises.
notes.analogy: A rubber duck is a duck in shape, but not if your code expects it to fly.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Collections.unmodifiableList(xs) returns a List whose add() throws UnsupportedOperationException. What is the design problem, and the better design?
notes.back: A Liskov violation: callers holding a List can't trust add(). Better: a separate read-only interface, like Kotlin List vs MutableList or C# IReadOnlyList.
notes.extra: Note: this is also an interface segregation problem: readers are forced to see mutators.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.text: Liskov substitution principle (LSP) contract rules for a subtype: preconditions may be {{c1::no stronger}} than the base's; postconditions may be {{c2::no weaker}}; the base's {{c3::invariants}} must hold; no {{c4::new exceptions}} callers don't expect.
notes.extra: Example: Account.withdraw accepts any amount ≤ balance; a subtype that also requires amount ≤ 500 strengthens the precondition and breaks callers.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Code review: callers contain if (shape instanceof Square) {...} before calling resize(). What does that signal?
notes.back: A Liskov violation: a subtype isn't substitutable, so callers defend against it. That also breaks the open/closed principle, since each new subtype adds a branch.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: How does the Liskov substitution principle (LSP) apply beyond classes, e.g. two implementations of a BlobStore interface?
notes.back: Any implementation behind an interface must keep the same behavioural promises. If one store is strongly consistent and another eventually consistent, callers relying on read-after-write break.
notes.extra: Architect angle: state semantics (consistency, ordering, idempotency) in the interface contract, not just method names.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Interface segregation principle (ISP): what does it say?
notes.back: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they don't use. Split fat interfaces into role interfaces shaped by each client's needs.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: interface MultiFunctionDevice { print(); scan(); fax(); staple(); }. A BasicPrinter must implement it. What goes wrong, and the fix?
notes.back: BasicPrinter must stub scan()/fax() to throw. Split into role interfaces Printer, Scanner, Fax; a real all-in-one implements all three.
notes.analogy: A job ad asking a typist to also fly helicopters: most applicants must fake it.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: def send_report(db: Database) only ever calls db.fetch_report_rows(), but Database has 40 methods. Why does the interface segregation principle (ISP) matter here?
notes.back: The function claims to need everything: test fakes must cover 40 methods, and any change to Database touches it. Depend on a narrow ReportSource protocol instead.
notes.extra: In Python/TypeScript: a structural Protocol or type lets the real Database satisfy it without changes.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: When does the interface segregation principle (ISP) go too far?
notes.back: When every method gets its own interface ("interface soup"). Split by client role, not per method: methods one client always uses together stay together.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Dependency inversion principle (DIP): what does it say?
notes.back: High-level policy must not depend on low-level detail; both depend on an abstraction, and the abstraction is owned by the high-level side.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: InvoiceService does this.repo = new MySqlInvoiceRepository(). Which principle is broken, and what is the fix?
notes.back: The dependency inversion principle: business policy depends on a database detail. Define InvoiceRepository in the domain package, implement it in infrastructure, and pass it in.
notes.analogy: A lamp with a plug instead of wires soldered into the wall: the socket standard belongs to the house, any lamp can fit.
notes.extra: Payoff: unit tests use an in-memory repository; swapping MySQL touches one class.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Dependency inversion principle (DIP): why must the interface live in the high-level package, not next to the implementation?
notes.back: If InvoiceRepository lives in the MySQL package, the domain still imports the infrastructure package: the arrow hasn't flipped. Ownership is what inverts it.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Dependency inversion (DIP) vs dependency injection (DI) vs inversion of control (IoC): how to tell them apart?
notes.back: DIP: a design rule on which way source dependencies point. DI: a technique, passing collaborators in instead of creating them. IoC: a framework calls your code.
notes.extra: Independent: you can inject a concrete MySqlRepo (DI without DIP), or invert dependencies with a hand-wired main() and no container.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: When is introducing an interface for the dependency inversion principle (DIP) overkill?
notes.back: When the dependency is stable and never varies or crosses a boundary: String, List, a pure PriceFormatter. An IStringUtils with one implementation forever is just indirection.
notes.extra: Invert at volatile or slow boundaries: databases, networks, clocks, vendors.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Single responsibility (SRP) vs interface segregation (ISP): how to tell them apart?
notes.back: SRP looks from the implementer's side: what forces this module to change? ISP looks from the client's side: what does this caller need to see?
notes.extra: Example: one cohesive UserRepository (fine by SRP) can still expose a read-only role interface to reporting code (ISP).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: How does the Liskov substitution principle (LSP) relate to the open/closed principle (OCP)?
notes.back: OCP extends behaviour by adding new subtypes behind an abstraction; LSP is what makes that safe. A non-substitutable subtype forces callers to branch, re-opening them for modification.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Main critique of SOLID as commonly practised?
notes.back: The principles are vague, so applied as rules they breed tiny classes and one-implementation interfaces. They are heuristics for managing change, not goals in themselves.
notes.extra: Alternative: Dan North's CUPID describes properties (composable, Unix philosophy, predictable, idiomatic, domain-based) rather than rules.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Scenario: every new payment provider means editing the switch in PaymentProcessor.charge(). Which principle applies?
notes.back: The open/closed principle (OCP): add a PaymentGateway extension point so a new provider is a new class, not an edit.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Scenario: a unit test of ReportService needs a running SMTP server. Which principle applies?
notes.back: The dependency inversion principle (DIP): the service depends on a concrete mailer. Depend on a Notifier abstraction and inject a fake.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Scenario: CachedRepository extends Repository, and its save() throws "not supported". Which principle applies?
notes.back: The Liskov substitution principle (LSP): callers of Repository can't rely on save(). Model read-only access as its own interface.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Scenario: the mobile app's client library must be rebuilt whenever an admin-only method changes on UserApi. Which principle applies?
notes.back: The interface segregation principle (ISP): split UserApi into a public user interface and an admin interface.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Scenario: a change to VAT rules forced a redeploy, and a regression, in PDF invoice layout. Which principle applies?
notes.back: The single responsibility principle (SRP): tax calculation (finance's rules) and layout (design's rules) change for different actors and live in one class.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Sandi Metz: someone extracted buildReport(data, isMonthly, includeTax, legacyFormat) from two reports, and every new report adds a flag. What is her remedy?
notes.back: Go back: inline the abstraction into each caller, delete what each doesn't use, then look for the real shared concept. "Duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction."
notes.analogy: A one-size-fits-all suit altered for each wearer until it fits nobody; recut it from cloth.
notes.extra: Why it persists: sunk cost. Each new developer assumes the abstraction must be right and adds one more parameter.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: KISS (keep it simple, stupid): concrete example of violating it?
notes.back: Building a configurable rules engine with a domain language for three discount rules that a ten-line if would handle. The engine itself becomes the hardest code to change.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.text: YAGNI (you aren't gonna need it): a team adds multi-currency support "in case we go international". Fowler's costs of such a presumptive feature: cost of {{c1::build}} (effort spent now), cost of {{c2::delay}} (real features ship later), cost of {{c3::carry}} (extra complexity slows every change), cost of {{c4::repair}} (when the real need arrives, it differs from the guess).
notes.analogy: Packing skis, a wetsuit and a tuxedo for a trip whose destination you don't know yet: you pay to carry them all the way.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Which kind of work does YAGNI (you aren't gonna need it) not forbid?
notes.back: Work that makes the code easier to change: refactoring, tests, clear names, deployment automation. YAGNI is about speculative features, not about design quality.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.text: Constantine's cohesion scale, worst to best: {{c1::coincidental}} (a utils.py of unrelated helpers), logical (grouped by category, e.g. all input handlers), {{c2::temporal}} (things done at the same time, e.g. initAll()), procedural, communicational (same data), sequential (output feeds the next), {{c3::functional}} (all parts serve one well-defined task).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: fetchUsers(mode) branches internally on mode == "fast" or "full". Which kind of coupling is this, and why is it a problem?
notes.back: Control coupling: the caller steers the callee's internal logic, so the caller must know how it works inside. A flag argument is the classic form; split into two functions.
notes.analogy: A back-seat driver telling the driver which pedal to press, instead of where to go.
notes.extra: Scale, best to worst: data, stamp, control, external, common (globals), content (reaching into internals).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: createUser("bob", "b@x.io", true, false, 3): which connascence, and how do you weaken it?
notes.back: Connascence of Position: callers must know the argument order and meaning. Use named arguments or a parameter object to reduce it to connascence of Name.
notes.extra:
createUser({ name: "bob", email: "b@x.io",
  isAdmin: true, verified: false, quota: 3 });

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Two services both treat status == 3 as "shipped". Which connascence is this, and the fix?
notes.back: Connascence of Meaning (convention): both must agree on what a magic value means. Use a shared named enum or string "SHIPPED", reducing it to connascence of Name.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: The signup service hashes passwords with SHA-256 + salt, and the login service must do the same. Which connascence is this?
notes.back: Connascence of Algorithm: both sides must implement the same algorithm. Put it in one place (a shared library or one auth service) so only one copy can change.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: email.setBody(b); email.send(); fails silently if the order is swapped. Which connascence is this, and why is it nasty?
notes.back: Connascence of Execution (order). It is dynamic, so the compiler can't catch it. Remove it by construction: mailer.send(new Email(to, body)).
notes.analogy: An envelope you must remember to fill before posting; a sealed letter handed over in one go can't be sent empty.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Connascence's rule of locality: how should strength relate to distance?
notes.back: The further apart two elements are (same function → class → module → service), the weaker their connascence must be. Strong connascence is fine inside one function.
notes.analogy: Whispering in-jokes is fine at the dinner table; across countries, you need a written standard.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: user.getName() also writes a "last accessed" row to the database. Which principle does this break?
notes.back: The principle of least astonishment: a getter should not have side effects. Readers and callers (loops, logging, debuggers) will call it freely and get surprises.
notes.extra: Other examples: equals() that isn't symmetric; a delete() that only marks a flag; Python list.sort() returning None trips people expecting a list.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::03 SOLID & Design Principles
notes.front: Scenario: an enum Role is checked with if role == ADMIN in 30 places, and a new AUDITOR role needs a subset of admin rights. Which principle is at stake, and what move helps?
notes.back: DRY (don't repeat yourself): the knowledge "who may do X" is scattered. Centralise it in a policy, can(user, Action.EXPORT), so a new role is one change.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: What problem do all the Gang of Four (GoF) creational patterns attack?
notes.back: A hard-coded new ConcreteClass() ties the caller to one class. They move the decision which class, built how out of the code that uses the object.
notes.extra: Why it matters: code that only knows an interface can be handed any implementation; code that calls new cannot.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.text: Gang of Four (GoF) creational patterns by what varies: the class created by one step of an algorithm → {{c1::Factory Method}}; a whole family of matching products → {{c2::Abstract Factory}}; how one complex object is assembled → {{c3::Builder}}; the class chosen by copying a configured instance → {{c4::Prototype}}; the number of instances (one) → {{c5::Singleton}}.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Factory Method: intent, in one line?
notes.back: Define an interface for creating an object but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate. The algorithm is fixed; the product it creates varies.
notes.analogy: A franchise manual says 'bake the house bread' at step 3; each branch decides which bread that is.
notes.extra: Shape: an abstract Creator calls its own createProduct() inside a template method; each subclass overrides it.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: A logistics app's planDelivery() is identical for road and sea, except one step needs a Truck or a Ship. Which pattern?
notes.back: Factory Method: planDelivery() calls an abstract createTransport(); RoadLogistics and SeaLogistics override it.
notes.extra:
Sketch:
abstract class Logistics {
  void planDelivery() { Transport t = createTransport(); t.deliver(); }
  abstract Transport createTransport();
}
class SeaLogistics extends Logistics { Transport createTransport() { return new Ship(); } }

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: A framework's Application.openFile() must create a document, but only the concrete app (drawing, spreadsheet) knows which Document subclass. Which pattern?
notes.back: Factory Method (the original Gang of Four (GoF) example): the framework calls createDocument(), and each application subclass overrides it.
notes.extra: Signal: a framework that owns the workflow but cannot know the product classes its users will invent.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: A legacy class calls new SystemClock() inside a method, so tests cannot control time. What is the smallest creational fix?
notes.back: Extract the new into a protected factory method createClock() and override it in a test subclass to return a fake clock.
notes.extra: Name: Feathers calls this Extract and Override Factory Method. Better long-term: pass the clock in through the constructor.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Simple factory (a static create(type) with a switch) vs Gang of Four (GoF) Factory Method?
notes.back: Simple factory picks the class with a parameter in one place. Factory Method picks it by subclass override, so new products need no edit to existing code.
notes.extra: In practice: a simple factory is often enough. It at least gathers the scattered switch statements into one function.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Which code smell says creation logic wants a factory?
notes.back: The same switch (type) or if/else chain around new repeated at several call sites, each edited whenever a new type arrives.
notes.analogy: Every shop keeping its own copy of the supplier list: one change, many places to update.
notes.extra: Example: if (fmt == "pdf") new PdfExporter() else if (fmt == "csv") … in the controller, the scheduler and the CLI.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Java's Collection.iterator(): which Gang of Four (GoF) creational pattern?
notes.back: Factory Method: each collection subclass returns its own Iterator implementation; callers only see the interface.
notes.extra: Same idea: Python's __iter__() and C#'s GetEnumerator().

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Effective Java's static factory method (List.of(), Integer.valueOf()) vs the Gang of Four (GoF) Factory Method?
notes.back: A static factory is a named constructor: it can cache, return a subtype or describe intent. It uses no subclass override, so it is not the GoF pattern.
notes.extra: Watch out: people say 'factory method' for both; ask whether polymorphism picks the class.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: What does Factory Method cost, and what is the modern lighter alternative?
notes.back: A creator subclass for each product, which gives two parallel hierarchies. Instead, pass a factory function (Supplier<T>, a lambda) to the constructor.
notes.extra: Example: new Pool(() -> new Connection(url)) varies the product with no PoolForPostgres subclass.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Abstract Factory: intent, in one line?
notes.back: An interface for creating families of related objects without naming their concrete classes, so products from one family are always used together.
notes.analogy: A furniture showroom sells 'the Victorian set' or 'the Modern set'. You pick the style once and never get a Victorian chair with a Modern sofa.
notes.extra: What varies: the whole family (look and feel, cloud vendor, database), chosen once.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Your app must render a whole consistent widget family (buttons, checkboxes, menus) for a macOS or Windows theme. Which pattern?
notes.back: Abstract Factory: a GUIFactory with createButton(), createCheckbox(); MacFactory and WinFactory implement it. Choose one at startup.
notes.extra: Payoff: no if (os == MAC) in widget code, and no mixed families.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: A multi-cloud tool needs matching BlobStore, Queue and SecretStore clients for AWS or Google Cloud, never mixing vendors in one deployment. Which pattern?
notes.back: Abstract Factory: CloudFactory with one creation method per client type; AwsFactory and GoogleCloudFactory each return a coherent set.
notes.extra: Wire it: read the vendor from config once, at the composition root, and pass the factory down.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Which signal suggests an Abstract Factory?
notes.back: The same platform or vendor check (if (theme == DARK)) repeated at every object creation, plus bugs where products from different families get mixed.
notes.extra: Fix: make the decision once by choosing a factory; everything downstream asks that factory.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: In Abstract Factory, which change is easy and which is painful?
notes.back: Easy: a new family (add LinuxFactory). Painful: a new product kind (createSlider()), which changes the interface and every existing factory.
notes.analogy: Adding a new furniture style is one new catalogue; adding 'lamps' to every style means redesigning all catalogues.
notes.extra: Rule of thumb: use it when the families grow, not the product list.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Java's AWT Toolkit creates native button, frame and menu peers for the current operating system. Which pattern?
notes.back: Abstract Factory: one Toolkit per platform returns a matching family of native peer objects.
notes.extra: Other anchors: javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory picks a parser implementation at run time; test suites swap an InMemoryRepositoryFactory for a database-backed one.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Factory Method vs Abstract Factory: how to tell?
notes.back: Factory Method: one method, overridden by a subclass, creates one product. Abstract Factory: a separate object with several creation methods for a family, passed in by composition.
notes.analogy: Factory Method: a chef who decides the side dish. Abstract Factory: hiring a whole kitchen of one cuisine.
notes.extra: Link: each method of an Abstract Factory is often a factory method.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Builder: intent, in one line?
notes.back: Separate the step-by-step construction of a complex object from its representation, so the same steps can produce different results or one valid, often immutable, object.
notes.extra: What varies: how a composite object gets assembled.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: A Pizza constructor has 9 optional parameters, and calls look like new Pizza(12, true, false, null, …). Which pattern?
notes.back: Builder: Pizza.builder().size(12).cheese().olives().build() names each choice and leaves defaults out.
notes.analogy: Ordering at a sandwich counter, item by item, instead of filling one form with 9 boxes.
notes.extra:
Sketch:
Pizza p = Pizza.builder()
    .size(12)
    .extraCheese()
    .crust(THIN)
    .build();   // validates, returns immutable Pizza

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: What are the telescoping constructor smell and the JavaBeans setter alternative, and why do both lose to Builder?
notes.back: Telescoping: overloads with 1, 2, 3… params, so call sites are unreadable. Setters: readable, but the object is mutable and half-built in between. Builder gives both readability and validity.
notes.extra: Classic source: Bloch, Effective Java, item 2.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Why is build() the right place for cross-field validation?
notes.back: It runs once with all parts known, so it can enforce rules like 'end after start' and the object never exists in an invalid state.
notes.extra: Pairs well with: immutable results; the builder is mutable scratch space, the product is not.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: You build Kubernetes manifests in Java with new PodBuilder().withNewMetadata().withName("web").endMetadata()…build(). Why is Builder a good fit here?
notes.back: A deeply nested object with dozens of optional fields: Builder lets you set only what matters, nest sub-objects fluently and get an immutable result.
notes.extra: Other anchors: Java 11 HttpRequest.newBuilder(), AWS SDK v2 PutObjectRequest.builder(), SQL query builders.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: In the Gang of Four (GoF) Builder, what is the Director?
notes.back: An optional object that knows the order of steps. The builder knows how to do each step, so one director can drive several builders.
notes.analogy: A recipe (director) can be cooked by different kitchens (builders) with the same steps.
notes.extra: GoF example: a rich text format (RTF) reader (director) feeds the same parse events to an ASCII, a TeX or a widget builder.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Java's StringBuilder: which pattern does it echo, and why?
notes.back: Builder: you accumulate parts in a mutable helper, then toString() produces the finished immutable String.
notes.extra: Same shape: Go's strings.Builder, .NET's StringBuilder.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: With named and default arguments (Kotlin, Python, C#), when do you still need a Builder?
notes.back: Rarely for plain optional parameters. Still useful for stepwise or conditional assembly, nested structures, or validation across many fields before the object exists.
notes.extra: Example: Pizza(size=12, crust=THIN) in Kotlin needs no builder; a query assembled in a loop from filters still does.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Go has no named arguments or overloading. What is its idiomatic substitute for a Builder?
notes.back: Functional options: NewServer(addr, WithTimeout(5*time.Second), WithTLS(cfg)), where each option is a function that edits the config.
notes.extra:
Sketch:
type Option func(*Server)
func WithTimeout(d time.Duration) Option {
    return func(s *Server) { s.timeout = d }
}

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Builder vs Abstract Factory: how to tell?
notes.back: Builder assembles one complex object step by step and returns it at the end. Abstract Factory returns several related objects, each immediately, in one call.
notes.extra: Question to ask: is the hard part 'which family?' (Abstract Factory) or 'how is this one thing assembled?' (Builder).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Prototype: intent, in one line?
notes.back: Create new objects by copying a configured instance, so the class and settings are picked at run time by which prototype you hold.
notes.analogy: A cookie cutter: shape it once, then stamp out as many as you like and decorate each one.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: A game level editor offers a palette of preconfigured enemies (an orc with 50 hit points (HP) and an axe, an archer with 30 HP) that designers stamp into levels. Which pattern?
notes.back: Prototype: the palette holds configured instances; placing one calls clone() and then tweaks position.
notes.extra: Why not subclasses: 'StrongOrc', 'WeakOrc' would be classes that differ only in data.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Which signal suggests Prototype rather than a factory?
notes.back: Many subclasses that differ only in configuration values, or objects that are expensive to set up (parsed, loaded, computed) and needed in slightly varied copies.
notes.extra: Example: a report template loaded from a database once, then cloned per customer and adjusted.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Prototype's main pitfall?
notes.back: Shallow copies: the clone shares mutable sub-objects (lists, maps) with the original, so editing one silently changes the other.
notes.analogy: Photocopying a form that has a sticky note attached: both copies still point to the same single sticky note.
notes.extra: Java note: Cloneable is widely considered broken (no method on the interface, shallow by default); prefer copy constructors or a copy() method.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Which mainstream language builds its whole object model on the Prototype idea?
notes.back: JavaScript: objects inherit directly from other objects through the prototype chain (Object.create(proto)), not from classes.
notes.extra: Lineage: taken from the Self language. Its class keyword is syntax over prototypes.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: How do immutable records change when you reach for Prototype?
notes.back: Copy-with-changes is built in (Kotlin data class copy(hp = 80), C# with, Python dataclasses.replace), and sharing is safe, so you rarely need a formal Prototype.
notes.extra: Still useful: a run-time registry of named prototypes, e.g. a palette or template catalogue.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Prototype vs Factory Method: how to tell?
notes.back: Factory Method needs a creator subclass per product, fixed at compile time. Prototype needs only a cloneable instance, which you can register and configure at run time.
notes.extra: Choose Prototype when new 'kinds' are really new data.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Singleton bundles which two promises, and which one causes most of the trouble?
notes.back: (1) Only one instance; (2) a global access point (getInstance()). The global access causes the trouble: hidden dependencies and no substitution.
notes.extra: Also: it mixes 'what I do' with 'how many of me exist', breaking the single responsibility principle (SRP).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: You need exactly one connection pool, but not a Gang of Four (GoF) Singleton. What do you do instead?
notes.back: Create one instance at the composition root and pass it in through dependency injection (DI). 'One' becomes a wiring decision, not a class property.
notes.analogy: One fire extinguisher per floor because the building plan says so, not because extinguishers refuse to be built twice.
notes.extra: Example: a Spring bean is singleton-scoped by default, yet any test can construct its own instance.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: When is a Singleton defensible?
notes.back: When the thing is truly unique per process and stateless or immutable, so nobody needs to swap it in tests. E.g. java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().
notes.extra: Other acceptable cases: a constant lookup table or a no-op logger. A mutable cache or config holder is the risky kind.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Why does a Singleton not give you 'only one' in a scaled-out service?
notes.back: It is one per process (in Java, per classloader). Five pods mean five instances. Cluster-wide uniqueness needs leader election or a distributed lock.
notes.extra: Classic bug: a 'singleton' scheduler that sends every email five times after scaling to five replicas.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: Safest way to write a lazy, thread-safe Singleton in Java?
notes.back: A single-element enum or the initialization-on-demand holder idiom; the Java virtual machine (JVM) guarantees safe, one-time class initialisation.
notes.extra: Avoid: hand-rolled double-checked locking; without volatile another thread can see a half-constructed object.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::04 GoF Creational Patterns
notes.front: In Python, why do you rarely write a Singleton class?
notes.back: A module is already a singleton: it runs once on first import and is cached in sys.modules, so module-level objects are shared.
notes.extra: Kotlin equivalent: object Config { … } declares a thread-safe singleton in one keyword. Both still carry the global-state cost.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.text: Gang of Four (GoF) structural patterns in one phrase each: {{c1::Adapter}} converts an interface; {{c2::Bridge}} splits abstraction from implementation; {{c3::Composite}} treats trees and leaves alike; {{c4::Decorator}} adds behaviour by wrapping; {{c5::Facade}} simplifies a subsystem; {{c6::Flyweight}} shares fine-grained objects; {{c7::Proxy}} controls access through a stand-in.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Adapter: intent, in one line?
notes.back: Convert the interface of an existing class into the one your client expects, so incompatible interfaces work together without changing either side.
notes.analogy: A travel plug adapter: the hair dryer and the wall socket stay as they are.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: A payment software development kit (SDK) exposes makeCharge(cents, isoCurrency), but your checkout code expects PaymentGateway.pay(Money). Which pattern?
notes.back: Adapter: AcmePayAdapter implements PaymentGateway, converting Money to cents and currency and calling the SDK.
notes.extra:
Sketch:
class AcmePayAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
  private final AcmeClient sdk;
  public Receipt pay(Money m) {
    return toReceipt(sdk.makeCharge(m.cents(), m.currency().code()));
  }
}

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Which signal says you need an Adapter?
notes.back: Conversion code for a third-party or legacy API (units, formats, exceptions) repeated at every call site, coupling your code to its shape.
notes.extra: Bonus: the adapter is the one place to change when you swap vendors, and the natural seam to fake in tests.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Object adapter vs class adapter?
notes.back: Object adapter wraps an instance (composition). Class adapter inherits from the adaptee and implements the target (multiple inheritance). Prefer the object adapter.
notes.extra: Why: it works with any subclass of the adaptee and in languages without multiple inheritance.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Java's InputStreamReader: which pattern?
notes.back: Adapter: it makes a byte-oriented InputStream usable where a character Reader is expected, decoding with a charset.
notes.extra: Other anchors: Arrays.asList() (array as a List), log4j-over-slf4j, which routes old log4j calls into the Simple Logging Facade for Java (SLF4J).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: When should you not write an Adapter?
notes.back: When you own both sides: just change the interface. Chains of adapters translating adapters usually mean the core model is wrong.
notes.extra: Smell: LegacyToV2Adapter wrapped by V2ToV3Adapter.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: In ports-and-adapters (hexagonal) architecture, where does the Gang of Four (GoF) Adapter appear?
notes.back: The port is an interface the core owns; each adapter (Postgres, Kafka, REST) converts between that port and a concrete technology.
notes.extra: Same move, bigger scale: the core never sees the vendor's interface.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Bridge: intent, in one line?
notes.back: Decouple an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently, joined by one reference rather than inheritance.
notes.analogy: A TV remote and the TV: new remotes and new TV models evolve separately, linked only by the infrared protocol.
notes.extra: What varies: two orthogonal dimensions, each in its own hierarchy.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Shapes (circle, square, …) × renderers (vector, raster, …) would explode into M×N subclasses like RasterCircle. Which pattern?
notes.back: Bridge: Shape holds a Renderer; shapes and renderers each get their own hierarchy, giving M + N classes.
notes.extra:
Sketch:
abstract class Shape {
  protected final Renderer r;
  Shape(Renderer r) { this.r = r; }
}
class Circle extends Shape { void draw() { r.drawCircle(x, y, radius); } }

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Notifications come as alerts, reminders and digests, and must go out by email, SMS or Slack. Which pattern keeps this from becoming 9 classes?
notes.back: Bridge: a Notification hierarchy (what to say) holds a Channel (how to send). Adding Teams is one class.
notes.extra: Signal: class names that are cross products, e.g. SmsReminder, SlackDigest.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Java Database Connectivity (JDBC): the same Connection/Statement API over Postgres, Oracle and MySQL drivers. Which pattern?
notes.back: Bridge: application code uses the abstraction (the JDBC API); vendor drivers are interchangeable implementations behind it.
notes.extra: Similar: the Simple Logging Facade for Java (SLF4J) API over Logback or Log4j backends.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: When is Bridge over-engineering?
notes.back: When only one dimension actually varies. The extra hierarchy adds indirection for flexibility nobody uses.
notes.extra: Approach: start with one hierarchy; extract the bridge when the second dimension appears.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Bridge vs Adapter: same 'wrap and delegate' shape, so how to tell?
notes.back: Bridge is designed up front so two sides can evolve independently. Adapter is retrofitted to make two existing, mismatched interfaces fit.
notes.analogy: Bridge: a building designed with standard sockets. Adapter: the plug converter you buy at the airport.
notes.extra: Ask: did we plan this split, or are we patching a mismatch?

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Composite: intent, in one line?
notes.back: Compose objects into trees for part-whole hierarchies, so clients treat a single item and a group of items the same way.
notes.analogy: An army: an order given to a division passes down to brigades, platoons and soldiers, and the general does not care which level receives it.
notes.extra: Key move: the container implements the same interface as its children.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: You want size() to work on one file and on a folder full of nested folders and files, with the same call. Which pattern?
notes.back: Composite: File and Folder both implement Node.size(); a folder returns the sum of its children's sizes.
notes.extra:
Sketch:
interface Node { long size(); }
record File(long bytes) implements Node { public long size() { return bytes; } }
record Folder(List<Node> kids) implements Node {
  public long size() { return kids.stream().mapToLong(Node::size).sum(); }
}

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: A shop sells products and bundles; a bundle can contain products and other bundles, and both need price() and weight(). Which pattern?
notes.back: Composite: Bundle and Product share an Item interface; a bundle sums (or discounts) its children.
notes.extra: Other domains: org charts (team cost), game scene graphs (move a group, children follow), menu trees.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Which code smell asks for Composite?
notes.back: Client code full of if (x instanceof Group) { loop over children } else { … }, repeated for every operation on the tree.
notes.extra: After: the recursion lives inside the composite, and clients make one call on the root.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: React component trees, the browser's Document Object Model (DOM) and AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) constructs: which pattern do they share?
notes.back: Composite: every node has the same type and may contain children of that type, so rendering, synthesis or traversal is one recursive call.
notes.extra: Example: CDK app.synth() walks stacks → constructs → resources uniformly.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Composite's design trade-off: where do add() and remove() go?
notes.back: On the shared interface: transparent but unsafe (a leaf must reject add). On the container only: safe but clients must know which is which.
notes.extra: Gang of Four (GoF) choice: transparency. Most modern code chooses safety.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Composite vs Decorator: both are recursive wrappers, so how to tell?
notes.back: Composite aggregates many children to represent a whole (sum, render all). Decorator wraps exactly one object to add behaviour to it.
notes.analogy: Composite: a box of chocolates. Decorator: one chocolate in gift wrap.
notes.extra: Ask: is the wrapper a group of things, or the same thing with extras?

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Decorator: intent, in one line?
notes.back: Attach extra responsibilities to an object at run time by wrapping it in another object with the same interface; a flexible alternative to subclassing.
notes.analogy: Clothing layers: shirt, jumper, raincoat. Each adds one property, any combination works, and you are still the same person inside.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: You must add gzip compression, encryption and buffering to an output stream, in any combination per use case. Which pattern?
notes.back: Decorator: each feature is a stream that wraps another stream, so you combine them by nesting rather than by subclass.
notes.extra: Pitfall: order matters. Compress before encrypting, or gzip finds nothing to squeeze.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Why not just subclass for each feature combination?
notes.back: n independent features give up to 2ⁿ subclasses (LoggingRetryingCachingClient…), fixed at compile time. Decorators combine n classes at run time.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Your Go service needs retries, request logging and an auth header on every outgoing HTTP call. Which pattern, and where does it plug in?
notes.back: Decorator: wrap http.RoundTripper. Each layer implements RoundTrip(req), does its job and calls the inner transport.
notes.extra:
Sketch:
type authRT struct{ next http.RoundTripper; token string }
func (a authRT) RoundTrip(r *http.Request) (*http.Response, error) {
    r = r.Clone(r.Context()); r.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+a.token)
    return a.next.RoundTrip(r)
}

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Go's bufio.NewReader(gzip.NewReader(file)): which pattern?
notes.back: Decorator: each layer is an io.Reader wrapping another io.Reader, adding buffering or decompression.
notes.extra: Same idea: Java's new BufferedInputStream(new GZIPInputStream(in)).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: What breaks when you wrap an object in a Decorator?
notes.back: Identity and type checks: the wrapper is not == the original, instanceof ConcreteThing fails, and methods outside the interface are hidden.
