notes.extra: Rule: decorate only through a small interface, and never let clients depend on the concrete class.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Python's @decorator syntax vs the Gang of Four (GoF) Decorator?
notes.back: Same spirit, different level: Python's wraps a function once, when it is defined. GoF wraps an object at run time, behind a shared interface.
notes.extra: Example: @functools.lru_cache and @retry add behaviour around a function without editing it.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Decorator vs Proxy: same structure, so how to tell?
notes.back: Decorator adds behaviour; clients stack them freely and pass in the wrapped object. Proxy controls access; it usually creates or manages the real object itself.
notes.analogy: Decorator: a phone case that adds a grip. Proxy: a receptionist who decides whether you see the director.
notes.extra: Ask: is the wrapper there to enrich the object, or to guard and stand in for it?

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Facade: intent, in one line?
notes.back: Provide one simple, higher-level interface over a complex subsystem, so common tasks need one call instead of a choreography of many.
notes.analogy: A hotel concierge: one request ('dinner and a taxi at 8') and they deal with the restaurant, the taxi firm and the cloakroom.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Every controller places an order by calling inventory, pricing, payment, shipping and email services in the same 6 steps. Which pattern?
notes.back: Facade: OrderService.placeOrder(cart) wraps the choreography; controllers make one call.
notes.extra: Signal: the same multi-step sequence of subsystem calls copied across clients.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: boto3's s3.upload_file() hides create-multipart-upload, upload-part and complete-multipart-upload. Which pattern?
notes.back: Facade: one high-level call over several low-level S3 operations, with chunking, threading and retries inside.
notes.extra: Note: the low-level client is still there when you need control, which is typical of a facade.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Does a Facade hide the subsystem from clients?
notes.back: No. It offers a simpler default path; clients that need fine control may still call the subsystem directly. It adds no new behaviour.
notes.extra: If you need to forbid direct access, that is a module boundary (package visibility), not the Facade pattern.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Facade's typical failure mode?
notes.back: It grows into a god object: every new use case adds a method until the facade knows everything and couples everyone.
notes.extra: Fix: several small facades, one per use-case area.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Which Gang of Four (GoF) pattern does a backend-for-frontend (BFF) or API gateway apply at architecture scale?
notes.back: Facade: one client-friendly endpoint aggregates calls to many backend services.
notes.extra: Watch: it is also where business logic sneaks in; keep it to composition and translation.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Flyweight: intent, in one line?
notes.back: Use sharing to support huge numbers of fine-grained objects cheaply: identical state is stored once and shared.
notes.analogy: A theatre's costume store: one costume per role, worn by whichever actor is on stage that night.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.text: In Flyweight, {{c1::intrinsic}} state (glyph outline, tree mesh) is context-free, immutable and shared; {{c2::extrinsic}} state (position, colour) depends on context and is passed in by the client.
notes.extra: Test: if two uses could disagree about a field, it is extrinsic.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: A text editor stores millions of characters, each as an object with font, outline and metrics. Which pattern cuts memory?
notes.back: Flyweight: one shared Glyph per character and font; the document stores only position and style per occurrence.
notes.extra: Result: about 100 glyph objects instead of 10 million.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: A game renders a forest of one million trees, but only 5 species, each with a 2 MB mesh and texture. Which pattern?
notes.back: Flyweight: share one TreeType per species; each tree keeps only x, y, scale and a reference to its type.
notes.extra: Signal: a heap profile dominated by many near-identical objects whose fields mostly repeat.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: In Java, why is Integer.valueOf(127) == Integer.valueOf(127) true but the same test with 128 false?
notes.back: Flyweight cache: Integer keeps shared instances for -128 to 127. Outside that range each call makes a new object, so == compares different references.
notes.extra: Lesson: compare values with equals(). Relatives: String.intern(), CPython's small-integer cache.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: What does Flyweight cost?
notes.back: Complexity and CPU: extrinsic state must be stored elsewhere and passed in on every call, and flyweights must be immutable. Worth it only at large counts.
notes.extra: Don't apply it before a memory profile shows the problem.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Flyweight vs Singleton: both share instances, so how to tell?
notes.back: Singleton: one instance of a class, reached globally. Flyweight: one instance per distinct intrinsic value (many in all), from a factory pool, immutable.
notes.extra: Also: Flyweight is a memory optimisation; Singleton is about identity and access.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Proxy: intent, in one line?
notes.back: Provide a stand-in with the same interface as the real object, to control access to it: delay, guard, cache or relay calls.
notes.extra: Smart reference: a fifth variant counts references or locks the real object on each access.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: A document viewer must open instantly even though page images are 40 MB each and most pages are never scrolled to. Which pattern?
notes.back: A virtual proxy: an ImageProxy knows only the size and loads the real image the first time draw() is called.
notes.analogy: A restaurant menu photo: you only cook the dish when someone orders it.
notes.extra: Same idea: object-relational mapper (ORM) lazy loading. Hibernate returns a proxy for order.getCustomer() and queries only on first access.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Only admins may call delete() on a Document, and you do not want auth checks inside the document class. Which pattern?
notes.back: A protection proxy: it implements Document, checks the caller's role, then forwards or throws.
notes.extra: Anchor: Collections.unmodifiableList() is a protection proxy: same List interface, but mutators throw.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: A gRPC-generated client stub lets you call inventory.getStock(sku) as if it were local. Which pattern?
notes.back: A remote proxy: it implements the service interface locally and turns each call into a network request to the real object.
notes.extra: Older relatives: Java remote method invocation (RMI) stubs, SOAP web-service clients.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Why is the remote proxy also a trap?
notes.back: It makes a network call look like a local call, hiding latency, partial failure and retries, so callers make chatty, fragile calls.
notes.analogy: A phone with perfect sound quality makes you forget your friend is on another continent, until the line drops.
notes.extra: Mitigation: coarse-grained interfaces, explicit timeouts, and names or types that admit the network (e.g. returning a future).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: A pricing service is slow and its answers stay valid for 5 minutes. Which pattern adds reuse without changing callers or the service?
notes.back: A caching proxy: it implements PricingService, returns stored results while fresh, and calls the real service on a miss.
notes.extra: Python: @functools.lru_cache applies the same idea to a function.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Why does Spring's @Transactional do nothing when a method calls another @Transactional method on this?
notes.back: Spring aspect-oriented programming (AOP) adds transactions through a proxy around the bean. A call on this skips the proxy, so no transaction starts.
notes.extra: Fix: move the method to another bean, or call it through the injected proxy.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::05 GoF Structural Patterns
notes.front: Mockito mocks, Java's java.lang.reflect.Proxy and Python's __getattr__ forwarding share which technique?
notes.back: Dynamic proxies: the proxy class is generated at run time and every call goes to one handler, which can record, check or forward it.
notes.extra: Payoff: one handler implements logging, security or mocking for any interface.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Chain of Responsibility: what varies, and how is the request passed?
notes.back: Which object handles a request. The sender hands it to the first handler; each handler deals with it or passes it to its successor.
notes.analogy: Calling a support hotline: you dial one number and get escalated from chatbot to agent to engineer without knowing who will finally help.
notes.extra: Decoupling: the sender never names the receiver, so handlers can be added, removed or reordered by configuration.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Every HTTP request needs authentication, rate limiting, logging and compression, configurable per route. Which pattern, and how does it look in practice?
notes.back: Chain of Responsibility as middleware: each handler does its part and decides whether to call next() or end the request.
notes.extra:
Anchors: Servlet Filter.doFilter(req, res, chain), Express app.use(), ASP.NET Core middleware.
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  if (!req.user) return res.status(401).end();
  next();
});

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: An expense system: team leads approve up to 1,000, directors up to 10,000, the chief financial officer (CFO) above that, and the thresholds change yearly. Which pattern?
notes.back: Chain of Responsibility: one approver per link, each approves within its limit or forwards. Changing limits or adding a level never touches the submitter.
notes.extra: Why not a big if/else? The cascade would live in the caller and every reorganisation would edit it.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: In a Kubernetes API server, a create request passes mutating admission, schema validation and validating admission webhooks; any one can reject it. Which pattern is this?
notes.back: Chain of Responsibility: an ordered chain of handlers, each of which may modify the request, reject it (ending the chain) or pass it on.
notes.extra: Same shape: email spam filters, servlet filters, logging frameworks passing a record up a logger hierarchy.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: In a browser, a click on a button with no handler goes to its panel, then the page. Which pattern, and along which structure?
notes.back: Chain of Responsibility along the containment tree: Document Object Model (DOM) event bubbling. Any ancestor may handle the event or call stopPropagation().
notes.extra: Also: the macOS responder chain and Java Swing's parent-component dispatch. The Gang of Four's own example was context-sensitive help.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Which code smell points to Chain of Responsibility?
notes.back: A long if/else-if cascade where each branch asks "can I handle this?", and the set or order of checks keeps changing or differs per configuration.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Chain of Responsibility: the two main risks?
notes.back: A request can fall off the end unhandled without anyone noticing, and debugging means tracing the whole chain to find who handled or swallowed it.
notes.extra: Fixes: end the chain with a default handler that logs or rejects; trace each link's decision. Long chains also add per-request latency.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Classic Gang of Four (GoF) chain vs a middleware pipeline: what differs?
notes.back: Classic: exactly one handler handles the request, then the chain stops. Middleware: every link may act, before and after calling the next one.
notes.extra: Consequence: middleware is a hybrid of Chain of Responsibility and Decorator, which is why the two are easy to confuse.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Command: what is the core move, and what does it make possible?
notes.back: Turn a request into an object (action, receiver, arguments). Now it can be stored, queued, logged, retried, undone or sent elsewhere.
notes.analogy: A restaurant order slip: the waiter doesn't cook. The slip can wait in a queue, be reprioritised, or be cancelled.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: A drawing editor needs unlimited undo and redo for move, recolour and delete. Which pattern, and what's the mechanism?
notes.back: Command with execute() and undo(): each action is pushed on a history stack; undo pops and reverses it, redo re-executes it.
notes.extra:
interface Command { void execute(); void undo(); }
history.push(cmd); cmd.execute();
// undo:
history.pop().undo();

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: A web shop must send emails and resize images in background workers, with retries. Which pattern underlies the job queue?
notes.back: Command: each job is a serialisable request object (type plus arguments) that any worker can execute later, retry, or move to a dead-letter queue.
notes.extra: Anchors: Java Runnable submitted to an ExecutorService; Celery and Sidekiq jobs.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: A game must let players rebind keys, and let the AI drive units with the same actions. Which pattern?
notes.back: Command: buttons map to command objects (Jump, Fire) instead of hard-wired calls; the AI issues the same commands to any actor.
notes.analogy: A universal remote: each button holds a programmable instruction, not a wire to one TV.
notes.extra: Bonus: a recorded stream of commands gives replays and network sync for free.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: A text editor lets users record a sequence of actions and replay it as a macro. Which pattern combination?
notes.back: Command for each recorded action, plus Composite: a macro is a command whose execute() runs its child commands in order.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Redux actions and command query responsibility segregation (CQRS) commands: in what sense are they the Command pattern?
notes.back: They reify a request as data ({type: 'addItem', id}) to log, replay or send. Unlike classic Command, the behaviour lives in a reducer or handler.
notes.extra: Payoff: Redux time-travel debugging replays the action log.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Which code smell points to Command?
notes.back: Callers wired directly to receiver methods, with undo, logging, queuing or retry code duplicated around each call site.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: When is a full Command class hierarchy overkill?
notes.back: When you only need to run something later, once, with no undo, queue or log. A function value (lambda, closure, Runnable) already is a command.
notes.extra: Keep the class when the command needs undo(), serialisation, a name in logs, or metadata like priority.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Command-based undo: what is hardest to get right?
notes.back: Each command must capture enough state to reverse itself exactly, and irreversible effects (email sent, card charged) can only be compensated, never undone.
notes.extra: In practice: sagas use compensating commands (refund) for exactly this reason.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Interpreter: what does it model?
notes.back: A small language's grammar as classes: one class per grammar rule, each with interpret(context). A sentence becomes a tree that evaluates itself.
notes.analogy: A recipe written as nested cards: "mix (A, B)" holds two cards; to cook, each card cooks its children, then itself.
notes.extra: Scope: Interpreter covers representing and evaluating sentences, not parsing text into the tree.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Marketing wants discount rules like cart.total > 100 AND tier == 'gold', editable without a deployment. Which pattern?
notes.back: Interpreter: parse each rule into an expression tree (And, Gt, Var, Const) and evaluate it against the cart.
notes.extra:
interface Expr { boolean eval(Ctx c); }
record And(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr {
  public boolean eval(Ctx c) { return l.eval(c) && r.eval(c); }
}

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: A monitoring tool lets users write alert conditions like cpu > 80 for 5m and not maintenance. Which pattern fits the evaluator?
notes.back: Interpreter: each operator and term is a node in an expression tree; evaluating the root against the current metrics answers "fire or not?".
notes.extra: Real world: feature-flag targeting rules, policy languages (Open Policy Agent's Rego), spreadsheet formulas.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Which code smell points to Interpreter?
notes.back: Business rules spread over dozens of config flags (minTotal, onlyGold, excludeSale) whose combinations keep multiplying: they are really a grammar.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: How does Interpreter relate to Composite?
notes.back: Its expression tree is a Composite: non-terminal rules (And, Plus) hold child expressions; terminals (Number, Variable) are leaves.
notes.extra: Often with Visitor: when you need several operations on the tree (evaluate, print, optimise), move them into visitors.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Interpreter: when should you not use it?
notes.back: When the grammar is large or speed matters: one class per rule explodes, and tree-walking is slow. Use an existing expression language, a parser generator, or compile to bytecode.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Iterator: what does it hide, and what does it enable?
notes.back: It hides a collection's internal structure. Clients traverse through one uniform interface, and several independent traversals can run at once.
notes.analogy: A TV remote's channel-up button: you step through channels without knowing whether they come from cable, satellite or the internet.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: A paged REST API returns 100 orders per page plus a continuation token. Callers should just loop over all orders. Which pattern?
notes.back: Iterator: hide paging behind next(), fetching the next page lazily when the current one runs out.
notes.extra:
Anchor: AWS SDK paginators.
def orders(client):
    token = None
    while True:
        page = client.list(token=token)
        yield from page.items
        if not (token := page.next): return

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: An org-chart tree must be walked depth-first in one feature and breadth-first in another, without changing the tree class. Which pattern?
notes.back: Iterator: one iterator per traversal policy, each keeping its own cursor (a stack for depth-first, a queue for breadth-first).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: External vs internal iterator: difference?
notes.back: External: the client pulls with next(), so it can stop early or interleave collections. Internal: the collection pushes each element to your function (forEach).
notes.analogy: External: you turn the pages of a book yourself. Internal: someone reads it aloud to you, page by page.
notes.extra: Trade-off: internal is simpler and safer; external is more flexible.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.text: Iterator in today's languages: Java {{c1::java.util.Iterator / Iterable (enables for-each)}}; Python {{c2::__iter__ / __next__ and generators}}; C# {{c3::IEnumerable with yield return}}; Go {{c4::range over iterator functions (iter.Seq, Go 1.23)}}.
notes.extra: Point: the pattern is now a language feature; you implement a protocol rather than design one.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Iterator: the classic pitfall?
notes.back: Modifying the collection while iterating over it. Java's iterators fail fast with ConcurrentModificationException; elsewhere results are undefined.
notes.extra: Also: lazy iterators over input/output (I/O) can usually be consumed only once; a second loop sees nothing.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Mediator: what problem does it solve?
notes.back: Objects that would all reference each other (many-to-many) talk only through one mediator, which encapsulates how they interact.
notes.analogy: Air-traffic control: pilots don't negotiate with every other plane; they talk to the tower, which sequences them all.
notes.extra: Result: each colleague knows one object instead of N−1 peers; the interaction rules live in one place.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: In a booking form, "one-way" disables the return date, a promo code updates the price label, and Submit enables only when all fields are valid. Which pattern?
notes.back: Mediator: widgets report changes to a form or dialog mediator, which holds the cross-widget rules and updates the others.
notes.extra: Without it: each widget references several siblings, and no single place shows the form's logic.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: In a game lobby, players, chat, ready buttons and a countdown timer must coordinate; today every component references every other. Which pattern?
notes.back: Mediator: a lobby object receives events ("player ready", "player left") and decides what the timer, chat and buttons do next.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: A checkout saga's orchestrator tells Payment, Inventory and Shipping services what to do next. Which pattern is this, at architecture scale?
notes.back: Mediator (orchestration): the services never call each other; the orchestrator owns the workflow.
notes.extra: Alternative: choreography, where services react to each other's events, is the Observer-style design. Trade-off: central visibility vs looser coupling.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Which code smell points to Mediator?
notes.back: Peer classes that each import and call several siblings to keep them consistent: "when X changes, update Y and Z" scattered across the peers.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Mediator: the main risk?
notes.back: The mediator becomes a god object: all interaction logic piles into one class that is hard to read and change.
notes.analogy: A team where every message must go through one manager: tidy at first, then the manager is the bottleneck.
notes.extra: Fix: one mediator per use case or screen, or push logic that concerns one colleague back into it.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Memento: what does it capture, and what is the encapsulation twist?
notes.back: A snapshot of an object's internal state so it can be restored later. Only the originator can read the snapshot; the caretaker just stores it.
notes.analogy: A sealed envelope from a bank: you keep it safe, but only the bank can open it and use what's inside.
notes.extra: Why the twist: undo code gets restore power without seeing or depending on private fields.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: A text editor wants undo by restoring earlier document states, without exposing the document's internals. Which pattern?
notes.back: Memento: before each edit, the editor (caretaker) asks the document (originator) for a snapshot, and hands it back on undo.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: A game checkpoint, a dialog's "Cancel changes" button, and a spreadsheet's what-if mode. Which pattern do they share?
notes.back: Memento: take an opaque snapshot before the risky part, and restore exactly that state if the user backs out.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Which code smell points to Memento?
notes.back: Undo or rollback code that reaches into an object's private fields (via getters, reflection or friend access) to copy and restore them.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Memento: main cost, and the usual mitigations?
notes.back: Memory and time: full snapshots of large state are expensive. Mitigate with delta snapshots, a bounded history, or Command-based undo instead.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::06 GoF Behavioural Patterns I
notes.front: Why do immutable data structures make Memento almost free?
notes.back: Every version is already a snapshot: keeping a reference to the old value is the memento, and structural sharing keeps memory low.
notes.analogy: Git commits: each commit is a full snapshot, yet storage stays small because unchanged files are shared.
notes.extra: Anchors: Redux time-travel debugging, Immer, Clojure's persistent collections.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Observer: what varies, and which dependency does it invert?
notes.back: The set of objects that react to a change. The subject knows only an observer interface; observers subscribe, so the subject never depends on them.
notes.analogy: A newsletter: the author doesn't know the readers; whoever subscribes gets each issue.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: A stock price feed must update a chart, a portfolio total and an alert rule, and more views will come. Which pattern?
notes.back: Observer: the feed is the subject; each view registers and gets update(price) on every change.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: After OrderPlaced, the shop must send an email, reserve stock and update analytics, without the Order module knowing those features. Which pattern?
notes.back: Observer as domain events: Order publishes the event, handlers subscribe. New reactions are added without touching Order.
notes.extra: Anchors: Spring ApplicationEventPublisher with @EventListener. Across services, the same idea becomes publish/subscribe over a broker.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: How do Kubernetes controllers learn about changes to Pods without polling the API server?
notes.back: Observer at cluster scale: informers hold a watch on the API server and call registered add/update/delete handlers, backed by a local cache.
notes.analogy: A doorbell instead of checking the porch every five minutes.
notes.extra: Detail: handlers usually just enqueue a key; the reconcile loop does the work, which tolerates missed or merged notifications.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: In a user interface (UI), which pattern links the model to its views so that changing the model repaints every view?
notes.back: Observer: views subscribe to the model. It is the core of Model-View-Controller (MVC), from Smalltalk-80.
notes.extra: Anchors: Document Object Model (DOM) addEventListener, JavaFX properties, RxJS observables, React re-rendering on useState changes.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Which code smell points to Observer?
notes.back: A class that, after changing, calls a hard-coded list of other modules (emailer.send(); stats.bump(); cache.clear()) that grows with every feature.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Observer: two classic costs?
notes.back: Update cascades that are hard to trace (who triggered this repaint?) with unpredictable order, and memory leaks from listeners never unsubscribed (the lapsed listener problem).
notes.analogy: A rumour mill: one remark sets off a chain of retellings, and nobody can say afterwards where it started.
notes.extra: Mitigations: unsubscribe in a lifecycle hook (React useEffect cleanup), weak references, or one-way data flow.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Observer: push model vs pull model?
notes.back: Push: the subject sends the changed data with the notification. Pull: it only says "I changed" and observers fetch what they need.
notes.extra: Trade-off: push is efficient but bakes in assumptions about what observers want; pull is generic but chattier and can read a later state.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Why can't you rely on the order in which observers are notified?
notes.back: The subject only promises "everyone subscribed gets told". If observer B needs A's result first, that is a hidden dependency: make it explicit (call A from B, or a Mediator).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: State: what varies, and how is it structured?
notes.back: Behaviour that depends on internal state. Each state is a class implementing one interface; the context delegates calls to its current state object, which can switch it.
notes.analogy: A vending machine's coin slot: the same button does nothing, dispenses or refunds depending on the machine's mode.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: An order can be Pending, Paid, Shipped or Cancelled, and cancel(), ship() and refund() behave differently in each. Which pattern?
notes.back: State: one class per status implementing OrderState; Order delegates to it. Illegal calls fail in exactly one place.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: A game character's input handling differs when Standing, Jumping, Ducking or Diving, and bugs keep appearing (jumping while ducking). Which pattern?
notes.back: State: each posture is a state object handling input its own way and choosing the next state, so impossible flag combinations disappear.
notes.extra: Before: booleans isJumping and isDucking that could both be true.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Which code smell points to State?
notes.back: The same switch (status) repeated in many methods, or boolean flags that can combine into illegal states.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: State: who decides the next state?
notes.back: Either the context (a central transition table) or the state objects themselves (each sets its successor). The second is more local but couples states to each other.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: State: when isn't it worth it?
notes.back: With few states and little behaviour each, or when transitions are pure data: an enum plus a transition table (or a workflow engine) is simpler.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: How does the typestate idea (e.g. in Rust) strengthen the State pattern?
notes.back: Each state is its own type, and transitions consume the old value, so calling ship() on an unpaid order fails to compile instead of failing at run time.
notes.extra:
fn pay(o: Order<Pending>) -> Order<Paid> { ... }
fn ship(o: Order<Paid>) -> Order<Shipped> { ... }

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connection: why is it the textbook State example?
notes.back: open, send and close mean different things in Listen, Established and Closed. The Gang of Four (GoF) book modelled each as a TCPState subclass the connection delegates to.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Strategy: what varies, and who chooses?
notes.back: A whole algorithm. Interchangeable algorithms share one interface; the client (or configuration) picks one and the context uses it without knowing which.
notes.analogy: Choosing a route in a navigation app: fastest, shortest or no tolls. The trip is the same; the routing algorithm is swapped.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: A backup tool must offer gzip, zstd or no compression, chosen in config. Which pattern?
notes.back: Strategy: a Compressor interface with one implementation per algorithm, selected at startup and injected into the backup job.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Sort one product list by price, rating or newest. Which pattern, and its standard-library anchor?
notes.back: Strategy: pass the comparison as an object or function, e.g. list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Product::price)) or Python sorted(items, key=...).
notes.extra: Anchor: java.util.Comparator and Collections.sort are the classic textbook case.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: A retry helper must support fixed delay, exponential backoff and exponential backoff with jitter. Which pattern?
notes.back: Strategy: a BackoffPolicy that returns the next delay; the retry loop stays identical while the policy is swapped per client.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Which code smell points to Strategy?
notes.back: A method shaped like if format == 'csv' … elif format == 'json' … where each branch is a whole algorithm and new options keep arriving.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: With first-class functions, when do you still write a Strategy interface and classes?
notes.back: When the strategy has several related operations, its own configuration or state, or needs a name for dependency injection and discovery. A single operation is just a function value.
notes.extra:
# a single-operation strategy is just a function
price = PRICING[customer.segment](cart)

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Strategy: costs?
notes.back: Clients must know the options exist to choose one; there is an extra object and indirection; and one interface must fit every algorithm, so some ignore parameters.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Template Method: what is fixed and what varies?
notes.back: The skeleton of an algorithm is fixed in a base-class method; subclasses override particular steps.
notes.analogy: A franchise restaurant's recipe card: the order of steps is fixed by head office, each branch chooses its local sauce.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: A data-import job always does open → parse → validate → save → report, but parsing differs for CSV, XML and Excel. Which pattern?
notes.back: Template Method: a final run() in the base class fixes the order; each importer overrides only parse().
notes.extra:
abstract class Importer {
  final void run(File f) { var rows = parse(f); validate(rows); save(rows); }
  protected abstract List<Row> parse(File f);
}

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Which Java Development Kit (JDK) class is a textbook Template Method?
notes.back: java.util.AbstractList: implement get(int) and size(), and inherited methods such as iterator(), indexOf() and equals() are built on them.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Template Method: abstract step vs hook?
notes.back: Abstract step: subclasses must implement it. Hook: has a default, often empty, implementation that subclasses may override to extend at that point (e.g. beforeSave()).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Where is Template Method in xUnit test frameworks?
notes.back: The runner fixes the sequence set-up → test → tear-down; you supply the steps. JUnit's @BeforeEach and @AfterEach are its annotation-based form.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Which code smell points to Template Method?
notes.back: Two or more classes with nearly identical long methods that differ only in a few steps: the shared order is duplicated and drifts apart.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Template Method: costs, and the modern alternative?
notes.back: Inheritance coupling: subclasses depend on the base class's call order (fragile base class) and get only one axis of variation. Alternative: pass the varying steps in as functions or strategies.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Visitor: what varies, and what must stay fixed?
notes.back: Operations over an object structure vary; the set of element classes stays fixed. Each operation is a visitor with one visitX method per element type.
notes.analogy: A tax inspector visiting different businesses: each business just lets the inspector in, and the inspector knows how to audit a bakery vs a garage.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: How does Visitor select the right code for an (element type, operation) pair?
notes.back: Double dispatch: node.accept(v) dispatches on the node's type, then calls v.visitCall(this), which dispatches on the visitor's type.
notes.extra:
class Call implements Node {
  public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.visitCall(this); }
}

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: A compiler's abstract syntax tree (AST) needs type checking, pretty printing, optimisation and code generation, with new passes added often. Which pattern?
notes.back: Visitor: one visitor per pass. Node classes stay untouched when a pass is added.
notes.extra: Anchors: javax.lang.model.element.ElementVisitor, the javac Tree API's TreeVisitor, Python's ast.NodeVisitor.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: A document of Paragraph, Image and Table nodes must export to HTML, PDF and Markdown, with more formats coming. Which pattern?
notes.back: Visitor: one exporter visitor per format, so each format's code sits together instead of being scattered across every node class.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Visitor: the central trade-off?
notes.back: Adding an operation is cheap (one new visitor). Adding an element type is expensive (every visitor needs a new method). Use it only when the element hierarchy is stable.
notes.extra: Name: this is the expression problem, seen from the object-oriented side.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Which code smell points to Visitor?
notes.back: Every new feature adds a method to every class of a stable hierarchy (toHtml, toJson, typeCheck), or instanceof chains over the same node types recur.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: Visitor: what does it cost in encapsulation?
notes.back: Visitors live outside the elements, so elements must expose enough state (getters) for every operation, weakening their information hiding.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::07 GoF Behavioural Patterns II
notes.front: With sealed types and pattern matching, how do you write a Visitor today?
notes.back: As a switch over a sealed interface with record patterns; the compiler checks the cases are exhaustive, so no accept/visit boilerplate.
notes.extra:
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
double area(Shape s) { return switch (s) {
  case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.r() * c.r();
  case Square q -> q.side() * q.side(); }; }

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: "Encapsulate what varies": how do you apply it when reading a design problem?
notes.back: Ask which part changes, or has several versions: algorithm, state, creation, interface, structure, recipients. Put that part behind an interface so the rest stays stable.
notes.analogy: Wall sockets: the appliance varies, so the house exposes a standard socket instead of wiring each device in.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Why is "which pattern can I use here?" the wrong first question?
notes.back: Patterns resolve forces you have actually seen. Start from the change you expect; apply a pattern when that variation is real, usually on the second or third case.
notes.extra: Symptom of getting it wrong: a StrategyFactoryProvider with one strategy.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Only one tax rule exists today; a second "might come someday". Introduce Strategy now?
notes.back: No: you aren't gonna need it (YAGNI). Write the direct code; extract a Strategy when the second rule actually arrives. Refactoring then is cheap.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.text: Gang of Four (GoF) aspects that can vary, behavioural: which object handles a request → {{c1::Chain of Responsibility}}; when and how a request is fulfilled → {{c2::Command}}; how and which objects interact → {{c3::Mediator}}; which private state is stored outside an object, and when → {{c4::Memento}}.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.text: Gang of Four (GoF) aspects that can vary, behavioural: objects that depend on another object, and how they stay up to date → {{c1::Observer}}; an object's behaviour as its state changes → {{c2::State}}; steps of an algorithm → {{c3::Template Method}}; operations applied to objects without changing their classes → {{c4::Visitor}}; how an aggregate's elements are traversed → {{c5::Iterator}}.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: A user interface (UI) kit must create matching buttons, menus and dialogs for either a light or a dark design system, and must never mix the two. Which pattern?
notes.back: Abstract Factory: one factory per theme creates the whole family, so the client cannot combine a dark button with a light menu.
notes.extra: Why not separate factory methods? Nothing would enforce that the products belong together.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: A plug-in framework's base Exporter runs the export workflow, but each plug-in must decide which writer class to create. Which pattern?
notes.back: Factory Method: the base class calls an overridable createWriter(); each plug-in subclass returns its own writer.
notes.extra: Often inside a Template Method: creating the product is one step of a fixed algorithm.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Building an HTTP request or a Kubernetes Pod spec with 15 optional fields, some combinations invalid, must read clearly and yield an immutable object. Which pattern?
notes.back: Builder: named step-by-step setters, validation in build(), then an immutable result. Avoids telescoping constructors.
notes.analogy: Ordering at a sandwich counter: add one ingredient at a time, and "wrap it" produces the finished sandwich.
notes.extra: Anchors: Java HttpRequest.newBuilder(), Lombok @Builder.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: A game spawns hundreds of enemies from preset templates that designers configure in data files; new variants must not need new classes. Which pattern?
notes.back: Prototype: keep configured template objects in a registry and clone one to spawn each enemy.
notes.analogy: A cookie cutter: shape it once, then stamp out copies instead of sculpting every cookie.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: A monitoring dashboard reads every source through MetricsSource.read(name), but a legacy plant controller only offers getReadingsXml(sensorId). Which pattern?
notes.back: Adapter: a PlantControllerSource implements MetricsSource calls the legacy API and converts the XML into your metric values.
notes.analogy: A travel plug adapter: the hair dryer and the socket stay as they are.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Bar, line and pie charts must each render to SVG, HTML canvas or PDF, without a class for every combination. Which pattern?
notes.back: Bridge: a Chart hierarchy (what to draw) holds a Renderer hierarchy (how to draw it), so 3 + 3 classes replace 3 × 3.
notes.analogy: Remotes and TVs built separately: any remote works with any TV through a standard infrared protocol.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: An org chart must report the total salary cost of any unit, where departments contain employees and sub-departments. Which pattern?
notes.back: Composite: Employee and Department share a cost() interface; a department sums its children recursively.
notes.analogy: A shipping crate's weight is the sum of what's inside, whether loose items or smaller boxes.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Add caching, retries and metrics around an existing HTTP client, in any combination per environment, without editing it. Which pattern?
notes.back: Decorator: each concern wraps the client behind the same interface; stack them in whatever order configuration asks for.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Teams keep calling six classes of a video transcoding library in the right order. They want transcode(file, preset). Which pattern?
notes.back: Facade: one simple entry point that drives the subsystem; experts can still use the classes underneath.
notes.analogy: A car's start button hides the fuel pump, starter motor and engine computer behind one press.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: A map editor renders millions of tiles that share a few dozen tile types, and memory explodes. Which pattern?
notes.back: Flyweight: share one object per tile type (intrinsic state: texture, walkability) and pass position as extrinsic state.
notes.analogy: Movable type: a printer owns one box of each letter and reuses it on every page.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: An image gallery should load full-resolution images only when they scroll into view, behind the same Image interface. Which pattern?
notes.back: Proxy (virtual proxy): a stand-in with the same interface that loads the real image on first use.
notes.analogy: A receptionist who answers for a busy executive and only fetches them when really needed.
notes.extra: Other proxies: remote (gRPC stubs), protection (access checks), caching.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: A checkout must apply one of several tax rules chosen per country at run time. Which pattern, and why not Template Method?
notes.back: Strategy: inject the country's TaxRule per order. Template Method would fix the rule by subclass, so one checkout object couldn't switch rules.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Several continuous integration (CI) jobs all run checkout → build → test → publish; only build and publish differ per language. Which pattern, and why not Strategy?
notes.back: Template Method: the shared part is the sequence, so fix it once and let each job fill in its steps. Strategy swaps a whole algorithm.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: A vending machine's insert-coin, select and refund behave differently when Idle, HasMoney, Dispensing or OutOfStock. Which pattern?
notes.back: State: the behaviour depends on the mode and the machine changes mode itself.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Several dashboards must refresh when a sensor reading changes, and the sensor code must not know about dashboards. Which pattern?
notes.back: Observer: dashboards subscribe to the sensor, which notifies whoever is listening.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: A smart-home app must schedule "heater on" for 6 am, log every action, and let users undo the last one. Which pattern?
notes.back: Command: each action is an object that can wait in a scheduler, be written to a log, and carry its own undo().

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Incoming support emails go to a spam filter, then an auto-responder for common questions, then team routing; any stage may finish the job. Which pattern?
notes.back: Chain of Responsibility: each stage handles the email or passes it on; stages can be reordered without changing the mail receiver.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: In a flight-search page, the date picker, passenger counter, fare filter and results list all affect each other. Which pattern?
notes.back: Mediator: the page controller receives every widget change and updates the others, so widgets don't reference each other.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: A photo editor offers "Compare with original" and "Revert" without exposing the image's internal layers. Which pattern?
notes.back: Memento: take an opaque snapshot when editing starts; restore from it on revert.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: A library must let callers stream rows from a 10 GB CSV file with an ordinary for-loop, without loading it into memory. Which pattern?
notes.back: Iterator, usually a generator: yield one row at a time, reading the file lazily.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: A security team wants access rules like role == 'admin' or (team == owner and hour < 18) stored in a database. Which pattern evaluates them?
notes.back: Interpreter: parse each rule into an expression tree once, then evaluate it against the request context.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: A cloud cost tool walks an infrastructure model (network, subnet, virtual machine, database) to compute cost, check compliance and draw diagrams. Node types rarely change; new analyses arrive monthly. Which pattern?
notes.back: Visitor (or a sealed-type switch): each analysis is one visitor over a stable set of node types.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Diagnose: "The same if (status == ...) appears in nine methods of Subscription." What varies, and which pattern?
notes.back: Behaviour by state varies → State: one class per status, so each status's rules sit together.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Diagnose: "Adding a Slack notification meant editing the Order service again." What varies, and which pattern?
notes.back: Who reacts to an order varies → Observer (domain events): Order publishes; the Slack notifier subscribes.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Diagnose: "Four importers are copy-pasted; they differ only in how they parse." What varies, and which pattern?
notes.back: One step of a fixed sequence varies → Template Method, or a parse Strategy passed to one shared importer.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Diagnose: "Each new report format adds a method to all twelve node classes." What varies, and which pattern?
notes.back: Operations over a stable structure vary → Visitor (or pattern matching over sealed types).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Strategy vs State: the class diagrams are identical. How do you tell them apart?
notes.back: Strategy: the client chooses the algorithm and the strategies don't know each other. State: the object changes its own state as it runs, and states know their successors.
notes.analogy: Strategy is choosing a golf club before the shot. State is a traffic light changing by itself.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Strategy vs Template Method: key difference?
notes.back: Strategy varies the whole algorithm by composition, swappable at run time. Template Method varies steps by inheritance, fixed when the subclass is chosen.
notes.analogy: Strategy: hire a different caterer for the whole meal. Template Method: keep the set menu's order and swap one course.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Strategy vs Command: both wrap behaviour in an object. How do they differ?
notes.back: Strategy is how to do a task the context already performs (interchangeable algorithms). Command is what to do: a request to execute later, queue, log or undo.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Command vs Memento for undo: how do they differ?
notes.back: Command stores the operation and reverses it: small, but needs inverse logic. Memento stores a snapshot and restores it: simple, but memory-hungry.
notes.analogy: Command is a receipt you can refund; Memento is a photo of the room before the party.
notes.extra: Combined: a command can save a memento of just what it touches, then restore it in undo().

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Observer vs Mediator: how do they differ?
notes.back: Observer: one-to-many broadcast; the subject doesn't know who listens or what they do. Mediator: many-to-many coordination; the mediator knows its colleagues and holds the rules.
notes.analogy: Observer is a radio broadcast: anyone tuned in hears it. Mediator is a wedding planner who coordinates caterer, band and florist with each other.
notes.extra: Combined: colleagues often notify the mediator through Observer.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Mediator vs Facade: both sit in the middle. How do they differ?
notes.back: Facade simplifies a subsystem one way; the subsystem doesn't know it exists. Mediator coordinates both ways; colleagues know it and talk only to it.
notes.analogy: Facade is a hotel concierge you ask for things. Mediator is an air-traffic controller everyone reports to and takes orders from.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Chain of Responsibility vs Decorator: both are chains of wrappers. How do they differ?
notes.back: Decorator: every link adds behaviour and always forwards. Chain of Responsibility: a link may handle the request and stop the chain.
notes.analogy: Decorator is layers of clothing: you wear every layer. Chain is a row of help desks: the first one that can help keeps you.
notes.extra: Middleware blurs the two: links wrap behaviour around next() and can also short-circuit.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Classic Visitor vs pattern matching on sealed types: when is the classic form still the better choice?
notes.back: When the language lacks sealed types, when visitors share default traversal by inheriting a base visitor, or when third parties must add operations to a library's tree.
notes.extra: Otherwise: a sealed-type switch is shorter and gets exhaustiveness checks from the compiler.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Iterator class vs generator: when do you write the explicit class?
notes.back: A generator is a function with yield; the language builds the iterator. Write a class when you need extra operations (peek, remove, reset) or explicit cursor state.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Interpreter vs a parser library: which job does each do?
notes.back: A parser library (ANTLR, parser combinators) turns text into a tree. Interpreter represents and evaluates that tree. Real languages need both; hand-roll only tiny grammars.
notes.analogy: The parser diagrams the sentence; the interpreter acts on what it means.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.text: Patterns that usually appear together: a Composite tree is walked by an {{c1::Iterator}} and processed by a {{c2::Visitor}}; a Command saves a {{c3::Memento}} to support undo; an Abstract Factory is implemented with {{c4::Factory Methods}} and its concrete factory is often a {{c5::Singleton}}.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Why do Composite, Iterator and Visitor so often appear together?
notes.back: Composite gives a uniform tree; Iterator walks it without exposing its shape; Visitor runs new operations on each node. Compilers and document models use all three.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Why does a concrete Abstract Factory often end up as a Singleton?
notes.back: An application usually needs only one factory per product family (one theme, one platform), so a single shared instance is natural. Today a dependency injection (DI) container usually provides it.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: How do Interpreter and Visitor combine?
notes.back: Interpreter gives the grammar's tree; when several operations (evaluate, print, optimise) are needed, they move out of the node classes into visitors.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::08 Choosing a Pattern: Scenario to Pattern
notes.front: Why are State objects often shared as Flyweights?
notes.back: When a state class holds no data of its own (everything is in the context), one instance per state can serve every context object.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: switch (employee.type) appears in pay(), bonus() and title(). Which refactoring?
notes.back: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism: one subclass (or strategy) per type, each overriding the methods. One switch survives, in the factory that picks the class.
notes.extra:
Smell: Repeated Switches. A single switch in one place is fine; the duplication of the same switch is the problem.
class Engineer extends Employee {
  pay() { return this.base * 1.1; }
}

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: An order's status field moves draft → paid → shipped, and every method branches on it. Why can't you use subclasses DraftOrder, PaidOrder?
notes.back: An object cannot change its class at runtime. Move the varying behaviour into a State object the order holds and swaps on each transition.
notes.analogy: A person doesn't become a different human when promoted; they change the badge they carry.
notes.extra: Kerievsky's name: Replace State-Altering Conditionals with State.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Replace Type Code with Subclasses vs with State/Strategy: which question decides?
notes.back: Does the type change during the object's life? Fixed for life → subclasses. Changes, or the class already has subclasses for another reason → State/Strategy field.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: A loan's capital() method branches on loan type with long, different formulas. Kerievsky's refactoring?
notes.back: Replace Conditional Logic with Strategy: extract each formula into a strategy class; the loan delegates capital() to its strategy.
notes.extra: When not: two short branches that never grow. Strategy adds a class per branch; pay that only when the variants are real.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: (startDate, endDate) are passed together to five functions. What refactoring, and what usually happens next?
notes.back: Introduce Parameter Object (DateRange). Next, behaviour moves onto it (contains(), overlaps()), so it becomes a real value object.
notes.extra: Smell: Data Clumps. The parameter object's real payoff is the behaviour it attracts, not the shorter signature.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Fowler's quick test for whether a group of fields is a Data Clump?
notes.back: Delete one of them. If the others no longer make sense on their own, they belong together in an object.
notes.extra: Example: street, city, postcode: without the city the postcode is a stray string → Address.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: if (priority == "high" || priority == "rush") appears in many places. Which refactoring?
notes.back: Replace Primitive with Object: a Priority class with higherThan(), ordering and validation, so comparisons live in one place.
notes.extra: Signal: the moment you write logic about a primitive (compare, format, validate), it wants to be a type.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: new Employee(name, "E"): the type code is passed to a constructor. Why replace it with createEngineer(name)?
notes.back: Replace Constructor with Factory Function: a factory can have a descriptive name and can return a subclass or cached instance; a constructor can do neither.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: A Loan class has five overloaded constructors and callers guess which one to call. Kerievsky's fix?
notes.back: Replace Constructors with Creation Methods: intention-revealing static methods such as Loan.newTermLoan(...) and Loan.newRevolver(...).
notes.extra: Companion: Chain Constructors, so all creation paths funnel through one full constructor.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Code builds an XML document with dozens of new Node() / parent.add(child) calls and keeps forgetting to attach children. Which refactoring?
notes.back: Encapsulate Composite with Builder: a builder with addChild()/addSibling()/up() builds the tree and hides the wiring.
notes.extra:
b = TagBuilder("order")
b.addChild("item").addAttr("id", 7)
b.addSibling("item")
xml = b.toXml()

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Code builds HTML by string concatenation: "<ul>" + items + "</ul>", with tag-closing bugs. Kerievsky's refactoring?
notes.back: Replace Implicit Tree with Composite: model tags as nodes in a tree that render themselves, so nesting and closing are structural, not textual.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: TextNode has flags stripHtml, decodeEntities, trim, each an if in toString(). Which refactoring?
notes.back: Move Embellishment to Decorator: keep the core class plain; each optional extra becomes a wrapper you stack only when needed.
notes.analogy: Instead of a coffee machine with a switch for every topping, you add toppings to the cup.
notes.extra: When not: embellishments that must run in a strict order or share state; decorator stacks then hide subtle ordering bugs.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Code that handles one item and code that handles a list of items do almost the same thing (if (spec != null) … else for (s : specs)). Kerievsky's refactoring?
notes.back: Replace One/Many Distinctions with Composite: a composite of specs is itself a spec, so callers always handle exactly one thing.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Two report subclasses have near-identical render() methods that differ in a few lines. Which refactoring?
notes.back: Form Template Method: extract the differing lines into methods with the same signature, then pull the now-identical skeleton up into the superclass.
notes.extra: Modern alternative: pass the varying steps as functions instead of subclassing.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: A servlet dispatches with a 40-branch if (action.equals("save")) … else if …. Kerievsky's refactoring?
notes.back: Replace Conditional Dispatcher with Command: one command object per action in a map keyed by name; the dispatcher looks up and calls execute().
notes.extra: Bonus: new actions can be registered without editing the dispatcher (open–closed).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: A TestResult class directly calls ui.update() and logger.write() when a test finishes. Kerievsky's refactoring?
notes.back: Replace Hard-Coded Notifications with Observer: let listeners register; the class just notifies whoever is listening.
notes.extra: When not: one fixed receiver that never changes; Observer then only hides the call graph.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: if (customer == null) name = "occupant"; is copied into a dozen callers. Which refactoring?
notes.back: Introduce Special Case (formerly Introduce Null Object): an UnknownCustomer that returns "occupant" and safe defaults, so callers stop checking.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: withdraw() returns -1 on insufficient funds and callers forget to check. Which refactoring, and when not?
notes.back: Replace Error Code with Exception, so the failure can't be silently ignored. Not for expected, frequent outcomes; return a result type instead.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Code catches ResourceExhaustedException as the normal way to learn the pool is empty. Which refactoring?
notes.back: Replace Exception with Precheck: if the caller can cheaply ask first (pool.isEmpty()), check rather than throw. Exceptions are for the unexpected.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: priceOrder(text) parses a raw order string and computes the price in the same tangled loop. Which refactoring?
notes.back: Split Phase: phase 1 parses into an intermediate data structure; phase 2 computes from it. Each phase can be understood and tested alone.
notes.analogy: A compiler: lex and parse into a syntax tree first, then generate code from the tree.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: A for loop filters offices in India, maps to phone numbers and pushes into a result array. Which refactoring?
notes.back: Replace Loop with Pipeline: offices.filter(isIndia).map(o => o.phone). Each stage states one intent.
notes.extra: Fowler 2nd ed.: 'Loops' became a smell in its own right.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Fowler's heuristic for when to Extract Function in a long function?
notes.back: Whenever you feel the urge to write a comment explaining a block, extract the block into a function named after that comment.
notes.extra: Key idea: separate intention (the name) from implementation (the body). Length alone is the weaker signal.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Person has officeAreaCode, officeNumber, formatPhone(). Which smell and refactoring?
notes.back: Large Class with a hidden concept. Extract Class TelephoneNumber: fields with a shared prefix that change together are the clue.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Kerievsky's Compose Method: what does the result look like?
notes.back: A method made only of calls to well-named steps at one level of abstraction, readable like a table of contents.
notes.extra:
void add(Object e) {
  if (readOnly) return;
  if (atCapacity()) grow();
  addElement(e);
}

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity().getName() appears in many callers. Smell and refactoring?
notes.back: Message Chains. Hide Delegate: give Order a shippingCity() method, so callers stop depending on the whole chain's structure.
notes.analogy: Asking the receptionist to fetch the manager instead of walking the corridors to find her yourself.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Message Chains vs Middle Man: how are their refactorings related?
notes.back: They are opposites. Hide Delegate cures chains by adding forwarding methods; Remove Middle Man cures a class that is only forwarding methods. Find the balance.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: An abstract PaymentProcessorBase has exactly one subclass and hook methods nobody overrides. Smell and refactoring?
notes.back: Speculative Generality. Collapse Hierarchy and Inline Function/Class; delete unused parameters and hooks.
notes.extra: Test: if the only users of a hook are tests, it is speculative.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Java's Stack extends Vector, so a stack also exposes insertElementAt(). Smell and refactoring?
notes.back: Refused Bequest: the subclass doesn't want its parent's interface. Replace Superclass with Delegate: Stack holds a list and exposes only push/pop.
notes.analogy: Inheritance says 'a stack is a vector'. A stack only has one.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: A method uses far more of another class's data than its own (Feature Envy). Default refactoring, and the deliberate exception?
notes.back: Move Function to the data it envies. Exception: Strategy and Visitor deliberately separate behaviour from data so the behaviour can vary.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: getTotalOutstandingAndSendBill() returns a value and also sends an email. Which refactoring?
notes.back: Separate Query from Modifier: totalOutstanding() (no side effects) and sendBill(). Queries can then be called freely and cached.
notes.analogy: Asking your bank for your balance shouldn't also pay a bill.
notes.extra: Principle: command–query separation (Meyer).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: getCourses() returns the internal list, and callers add() to it directly. Which refactoring?
notes.back: Encapsulate Collection: return a read-only view or copy; add addCourse()/removeCourse() so the owner controls changes.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: A field is set only in one rare code path and is null the rest of the time. Smell and refactoring?
notes.back: Temporary Field. Extract Class for the field and the code that uses it; add a special case for the absent variant.
notes.analogy: A spare-tyre bracket bolted to every car, though only one car in ten carries a spare.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: A mutable global config map is written from several modules. First refactoring?
notes.back: Encapsulate Variable: wrap it in functions so every read and write goes through one place you can log, guard or make immutable.
notes.extra: Smell: Global Data. Encapsulation doesn't remove it, but you can then see and limit who changes it.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.text: Kerievsky: you can refactor {{c1::towards}} a pattern (partly, stopping when the design is good enough), {{c2::to}} a pattern (fully), or {{c3::away from}} a pattern (when it is overkill).
notes.extra: Point: a pattern is a destination you may only half-reach; the code, not the catalogue, decides how far.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: A Singleton config object is used by two classes and makes tests share state. Kerievsky's move away from a pattern?
notes.back: Inline Singleton: create one instance in the composition code and pass it to the two users as a parameter.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: Why does Kerievsky prefer refactoring to patterns over designing them in up front?
notes.back: Up-front patterns over-engineer for guessed needs; no patterns under-engineers. Refactoring adds a pattern when a real smell shows the need.
notes.analogy: Paving footpaths where the grass is already worn, not where you guess people will walk.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::09 Refactoring: From Smell to Pattern
notes.front: A method passes a StringBuilder down through recursive calls so each adds its part. Kerievsky's name for this?
notes.back: Collecting Parameter (Move Accumulation to Collecting Parameter): one accumulator object is passed into each step, avoiding many temporary results.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: OrderService does new SmtpMailer() inside a method, so tests send real email. What do you change?
notes.back: Constructor injection: take a Mailer interface as a constructor parameter. Tests pass a fake; production passes SMTP.
notes.analogy: A lamp with a plug instead of hard-wired cables: what powers it is decided where it's plugged in.
notes.extra:
class OrderService {
  constructor(private mailer: Mailer) {}
}

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Why is Service Locator (Locator.get(Mailer) inside a class) considered an anti-pattern?
notes.back: It hides dependencies: the constructor lies about what the class needs, and a missing registration fails at runtime, not compile time.
notes.analogy: A job ad that lists no requirements, then fires you on day one for lacking a forklift licence.
notes.extra: Diagnosis: you can't tell what to set up for a test without reading the body.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: What is the composition root in dependency injection (DI)?
notes.back: The single place, near the entry point (main, startup), where the whole object graph is wired. Only it knows concrete classes or touches the container.
notes.analogy: The switchboard in a building's basement: every room just has sockets.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Constructor injection vs property (setter) injection: when is property injection acceptable?
notes.back: Only for a truly optional dependency with a sensible local default, e.g. a logger defaulting to a no-op logger.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: A constructor now takes eight injected services. What does that tell you, and what is the fix?
notes.back: Constructor over-injection: the class has too many responsibilities. Split it or group cohesive dependencies behind a facade service. Don't hide them in setters.
notes.analogy: A recipe with 25 ingredients is usually two recipes.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Pure DI (hand-wiring in main) vs a DI container: when is hand-wiring enough?
notes.back: When the graph is small to medium. Pure DI is compile-checked and explicit; a container pays off with many objects, conventions and lifetimes.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: When is Service Locator defensible, according to Nystrom?
notes.back: For a truly global service like audio or logging in a game, with a null service registered by default so callers never get null.
notes.extra: Tension: the DI school still prefers injection; the locator buys convenience at the cost of hidden coupling.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: A NullLogger is fine. Why is a NullPaymentMethod that silently does nothing dangerous?
notes.back: Null Object fits when 'do nothing' is a correct behaviour. If absence must change the flow (stop checkout), a silent stand-in hides a bug.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Null Object vs Special Case?
