notes.back: Null Object: a do-nothing stand-in for absence. Special Case (Fowler): any subclass for a special situation, with real behaviour, e.g. UnknownCustomer billed on a default plan.
notes.extra: Other special cases: MissingCustomer, InfiniteQuantity, NaN in IEEE floats.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Why must a Money type not be a double?
notes.back: Binary floats can't represent 0.10 exactly, so sums drift. Store integer minor units (cents) plus a currency; adding USD to EUR throws.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Splitting €100 three ways with Money: what does Fowler's allocate() guarantee?
notes.back: No cent is lost or created: 33.34, 33.33, 33.33. Remainders are handed out one by one, so the parts always sum to the whole.
notes.analogy: Sharing ten sweets among three kids: someone gets the extra one, but nobody throws it away.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: A filter isOverdue && amount > 1000 is duplicated in a UI query, a validation and a batch job. When is a Specification object worth it?
notes.back: When the rule is reused and combined (and/or/not) or must be translated to SQL. A rule used once is just a function.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: When is a hand-written generic Repository<T> over an object–relational mapper (ORM) pointless?
notes.back: When it just forwards to the ORM's context, which already is a repository and unit of work. Write repositories per aggregate with domain-named queries, or none.
notes.extra: Smell: IRepository<T> with GetAll(), Add(), Update() that leaks IQueryable anyway.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Bloch: why does EnumSet.of(...) use a static factory instead of a constructor?
notes.back: It can return different subclasses: RegularEnumSet (a single long bitmask) for ≤ 64 constants, JumboEnumSet otherwise. Callers never know.
notes.analogy: Ordering 'a car' from a dealer who picks the compact or the van to fit your passengers.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.text: Bloch's static-factory naming conventions: type conversion {{c1::from}}; aggregation {{c2::of}}; possibly cached instance {{c3::getInstance / valueOf}}; guaranteed fresh instance {{c4::newInstance}}.
notes.extra: Examples: Date.from(instant), List.of(a, b), Boolean.valueOf(true) (cached, never new).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.text: Bloch's rules to make a class immutable: no {{c1::mutator methods}}; make the class {{c2::final}} (or constructor private); all fields {{c3::private final}}; {{c4::defensive copies}} of any mutable components.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Immutable Strings concatenated 10,000 times in a loop are slow. Bloch's general answer?
notes.back: Provide a mutable companion for multistep building (StringBuilder for String), while the value type stays immutable.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: InstrumentedHashSet extends HashSet counts added elements, but addAll of 3 items reports 6. Why?
notes.back: HashSet.addAll internally calls add, which is also overridden: each element is counted twice. Inheritance depends on the parent's self-use.
notes.analogy: Paying a waiter per dish carried, not knowing that a 'tray' order is still carried one dish at a time.
notes.extra: Fix: composition. A forwarding wrapper holds a Set and counts in its own add/addAll.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Bloch: 'design and document for inheritance or else prohibit it'. Concretely?
notes.back: Either document which overridable methods call each other (self-use) and test subclasses, or make the class final / constructors private.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Fluent interface vs Builder?
notes.back: Fluent interface is a style: method chains that read like a domain-specific language (DSL), e.g. jOOQ, Mockito. Builder is a creation pattern; it often uses that style.
notes.extra: Cost: fluent setters return this from commands, bending command–query separation.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: A builder lets you call build() before setting the required url. How does a step builder fix that at compile time?
notes.back: Each step returns an interface exposing only the next legal method: url() returns MethodStep, and only the last step has build().
notes.extra:
Request r = Request.builder()
  .url(u)      // UrlStep -> MethodStep
  .get()       // MethodStep -> BuildStep
  .build();

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Tests need an in-memory ID generator; production uses a database sequence. Fowler's Plugin pattern?
notes.back: Bind the implementation of an interface by configuration at startup, not in code, e.g. via Java's ServiceLoader or a config key.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: When is an object pool worth it, and when not?
notes.back: Worth it when creation is expensive or limited: database connections, threads, large buffers. Not for small objects in a garbage-collected language, where allocation is cheap.
notes.extra: Exception: C++ games pool particles to avoid heap fragmentation (Nystrom).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: A pooled database connection is returned with an open transaction. What bug follows, and the rule?
notes.back: The next borrower inherits that state (transaction, session variables, temp tables). Reset or validate every object on return.
notes.analogy: A rental car returned with someone's luggage still in the boot.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Bloch on lazy initialisation: when should you use it?
notes.back: Rarely: only when a field is costly and often unused. Otherwise initialise normally. For a static field use the holder-class idiom; it is thread-safe and lock-free.
notes.extra:
private static class Holder {
  static final Parser P = new Parser();
}
static Parser parser() { return Holder.P; }

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Ten user interface (UI) panels each subscribe to five model objects. What does an Event Aggregator change?
notes.back: Panels and models talk to one hub: publishers post events to it, subscribers listen to it. Wiring drops from 10×5 to 10+5.
notes.analogy: A notice board in the corridor instead of everyone phoning everyone.
notes.extra: Cost: the flow becomes implicit; you need search, not the call graph, to find who reacts.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Game Programming Patterns: what problem does the Game Loop solve?
notes.back: It decouples the progress of game time from user input and processor speed: the game keeps running when nobody presses a key, at the same pace on any machine.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Why do robust game loops use a fixed update step with a lag accumulator but render at a variable rate?
notes.back: Fixed steps keep physics deterministic and stable; rendering as often as the hardware allows keeps it smooth, interpolating between steps.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Update Method: a monster's update() spawns a new monster into the list being iterated. What goes wrong and the usual fix?
notes.back: Iteration skips or double-processes objects. Note the count at the frame start, or queue additions and removals until after the loop.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Player must be both physical and renderable, Decoration only renderable, Zone only physical. Why does inheritance fail, and which pattern fits?
notes.back: Mixes of capabilities force a diamond or duplication. Component: an entity is a bag of physics, graphics and input components.
notes.analogy: Lego minifigures: swap the hat, legs or tool without designing a new figure class.
notes.extra: Scaled up: entity–component–system (ECS) stores components in arrays processed by systems, which also helps cache locality.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Deep gameplay code calls audio.play("boom"), which blocks for disk I/O and fires 8 times in one frame. Which pattern?
notes.back: Event Queue: append the request and return; the audio system drains the queue later, merging duplicates.
notes.extra: vs Observer: Observer decouples who receives; a queue also decouples when.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Each frame you recompute every object's world transform from its parents, though few objects moved. Which pattern?
notes.back: Dirty Flag: mark an object dirty when its local transform changes; recompute derived data only when it is read and dirty.
notes.extra: When not: the derived data changes every frame anyway, or recomputing is cheap.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: The renderer draws the frame buffer while the game is still writing it, so the screen tears. Which pattern?
notes.back: Double Buffer: write to a back buffer, then swap it with the front buffer atomically when complete.
notes.analogy: A stage with two sets: the crew builds the next scene behind the curtain, then the stage rotates.
notes.extra: Beyond graphics: any simulation where all actors must read the previous state (Game of Life, AI updates).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Collision checks compare every unit with every other: \(O(n^2)\) for 5,000 units. Which pattern?
notes.back: Spatial Partition: a grid, quadtree or k-d tree indexed by position, so each unit is checked only against nearby ones.
notes.analogy: To find who's near you at a party you scan your room, not every guest in the house.
notes.extra: When not: a few dozen objects; the bookkeeping costs more than brute force.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: A game has 200 monster breeds as subclasses (Troll, Dragon…) and designers want to add more without a programmer. Which pattern?
notes.back: Type Object: one Monster class holding a reference to a Breed object loaded from data (health, attack, parent breed).
notes.analogy: One printed form, many filled-in copies: the breed sheet is data, not a new class.
notes.extra: Cost: behaviour per type is harder; data can set numbers, not new code.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::10 Beyond GoF: Modern Object Patterns
notes.front: Designers and modders must script spell behaviour safely. Why Bytecode rather than a Gang of Four (GoF) Interpreter tree?
notes.back: A flat instruction array run by a tiny stack virtual machine (VM) is compact, cache-friendly and sandboxed; tree-walking interpreters are slow and memory-hungry.
notes.extra: When not: if an embeddable language (Lua) fits, use it instead of building your own.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: validateNonEmpty(list) returns void; later code calls head(list) and still must handle empty. What does 'parse, don't validate' change?
notes.back: Return a stronger type: parseNonEmpty(list) → NonEmpty<T>. The check's result is kept in the type, so later code can't forget it.
notes.analogy: A bouncer who stamps your hand: inside, nobody checks your ID again.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: What is shotgun parsing, and why is it dangerous?
notes.back: Validation checks scattered through processing code. A failure discovered halfway leaves the program having already acted on bad input.
notes.extra: Fix: parse everything at the boundary into precise types, then process only parsed data.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: A contact must have an email or a postal address, or both. Why is {email?: Email, address?: Address} a bug magnet?
notes.back: It allows 'neither'. Model three cases instead: EmailOnly | PostOnly | EmailAndPost. The invalid state can no longer be built.
notes.extra: Principle: make illegal states unrepresentable (Minsky).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: Minsky's connection record has lastPingTime?, sessionId?, disconnectReason? plus a state enum. How do you restructure it?
notes.back: A sum type with one variant per state, each carrying only its own fields: Connecting | Connected(sessionId, lastPing) | Disconnected(reason).
notes.analogy: Instead of a form with every box for every case, a separate form for each case.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: isVerified and isPending booleans on a user can both be true. What's the type-driven fix?
notes.back: Replace the flag pair with one enumerated state: Pending | Verified | Rejected. Two booleans give four combinations; the domain has three.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: sendPasswordReset(email) must only go to verified addresses. How does Wlaschin enforce that with types?
notes.back: Distinct types UnverifiedEmail and VerifiedEmail; only the verification service can create a VerifiedEmail, and the function accepts only that.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: OrderQuantity must be 1–1000. How do you build a constrained type?
notes.back: A private constructor plus a smart constructor create(n): Result<OrderQuantity, Error>. Every existing instance is valid by construction.
notes.extra:
static create(n: number) {
  return n >= 1 && n <= 1000
    ? ok(new OrderQuantity(n))
    : err("out of range");
}

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: transfer(fromId: Guid, toId: Guid): a caller swaps the two arguments and it compiles. Fix?
notes.back: Wrapper (newtype) types: AccountId, CustomerId. Same runtime representation, but the compiler rejects mix-ups.
notes.analogy: Different-shaped plugs for different voltages: the wrong one won't go in.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: Typestate: how can an HTTP request type make 'add a header after sending' a compile error?
notes.back: Encode state in the type: Request<Unsent> has header() and send(); send() returns Request<Sent>, which has no header().
notes.extra: Common in: Rust (moves consume the old value), also phantom types in TypeScript, Scala, Haskell.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: validate → price → save → notify, and any step can fail. What is railway-oriented programming?
notes.back: Each step returns Result (Ok or Error). Composition runs the next step only on Ok; the first Error travels down the failure track to the end.
notes.analogy: Points on a railway: one switch to the siding, and the train never rejoins the main line.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: In a Result pipeline, when do you use map and when bind (flatMap)?
notes.back: map for a step that cannot fail (a → b). bind for a step that can fail (a → Result<b>); map would nest Results.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: Result vs exceptions: which failures go where?
notes.back: Expected domain outcomes (card declined, invalid input, not found) → Result, visible in the signature. Bugs and unrecoverable infrastructure faults → exceptions.
notes.extra: Wlaschin's warning: don't wrap every I/O error in Result; if nothing can handle it, let it panic.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: A sign-up form should show all field errors at once, but your Result chain stops at the first. Why, and what instead?
notes.back: bind short-circuits by design. Use applicative validation: validate fields independently and combine, accumulating a list of errors.
notes.analogy: A teacher who marks the whole exam, not one who stops at the first wrong answer.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: findUser(id) returns null for 'not found'. What does returning Option/Optional buy?
notes.back: Absence becomes part of the type, so the compiler forces callers to handle it (map, orElse) instead of crashing later.
notes.analogy: A parcel locker that hands you either a box or a 'nothing here' slip, never an empty hand you discover later.
notes.extra: Bloch: use Optional for return values, not for fields, parameters or collections (return an empty list).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: Partial vs total functions: head([]) crashes. Two ways to make it total?
notes.back: Narrow the input (head(NonEmpty<T>)) or widen the output (head(T[]): Option<T>). Narrowing pushes the check to the boundary.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: Shape = Circle | Rect | Triangle with a match per operation. What replaces the Gang of Four (GoF) Visitor?
notes.back: Exhaustive pattern matching: each operation is a function over the sum type, and the compiler flags every match that misses a new case.
notes.extra:
area = match shape:
  Circle(r)  -> pi * r * r
  Rect(w, h) -> w * h

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: How do algebraic data types (ADTs) replace the Gang of Four (GoF) State pattern for an order workflow?
notes.back: States become variants of a sum type and transitions a pure function (state, event) → state; invalid transitions fail the match.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: What is the expression problem?
notes.back: Object-oriented (OO) code makes adding new types easy but new operations hard; sum types make adding operations easy but new types hard.
notes.analogy: A spreadsheet of types × operations: OO fills it row by row, functional programming column by column.
notes.extra: Example: a Shape hierarchy gets a new Hexagon in one file; adding perimeter() touches every class.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: When does object-oriented (OO) polymorphism still beat a sum type with pattern matching?
notes.back: When the set of types is open: third parties add them without editing your code (plugins, user interface widgets, database drivers). Closed sets with growing operations favour sum types.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: Every database call repeats open-connection / begin / commit-or-rollback / close. Functional replacement for Template Method?
notes.back: A higher-order function that takes the varying step: withTransaction(tx => repo.save(order, tx)). Also called execute-around or the loan pattern.
notes.analogy: A library lends you the book and takes it back; you only decide what to read.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: Closures replace most Command objects. When should a command stay data instead of a function?
notes.back: When you need undo, logging, queuing, retries or sending it across a network: a function can't be inspected or serialised; a data record can.
notes.extra: Name: defunctionalisation. Redux actions are exactly this.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: A subscription-renewal job reads the database, decides who gets emails, and sends them, all interleaved. Bernhardt's restructuring?
notes.back: Functional core, imperative shell: the shell reads data, a pure core returns decisions (which emails), the shell executes them.
notes.extra: Seemann's name: the impureim sandwich: impure read, pure decide, impure write.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: Why does the functional core need almost no mocks in its tests?
notes.back: It has no dependencies, only inputs and outputs. Tests pass values and assert on returned values; the thin shell gets a few integration tests.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: calculateLateFee(invoice) reads DateTime.Now inside. Why is that a problem and the fix?
notes.back: It's impure: the same input gives different outputs, so tests are flaky. Pass the time in: calculateLateFee(invoice, today).
notes.analogy: A recipe that says 'bake until it feels right today' can't be checked by anyone else.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: How does Wlaschin model a 'place order' workflow as types?
notes.back: As a pipeline of functions between states: UnvalidatedOrder → ValidatedOrder → PricedOrder → events. Each type documents what has been checked.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: Wlaschin: how do you do dependency injection without objects?
notes.back: Pass dependencies as the first parameters, then partially apply them in the composition root, leaving a function of just the input.
notes.extra:
let placeOrder checkProduct getPrice order = ...
let placeOrderLive = placeOrder dbCheck dbPrice

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: Why does Wlaschin's workflow return events (OrderPlaced, AcknowledgmentSent) instead of calling billing directly?
notes.back: The workflow stays pure and decoupled: it states what happened, and the shell decides who to notify.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::11 Functional & Type-Driven Design
notes.front: Where do data transfer objects (DTOs) fit in Wlaschin's design?
notes.back: At the trust boundary: untrusted DTOs are parsed into domain types on the way in and built from them on the way out. Domain types never serialise directly.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: OrderManager is 4,000 lines, every feature touches it, and its tests take minutes. Diagnosis and first remedy?
notes.back: God Object (the Blob). Find clusters of fields and methods used together and Extract Class; move behaviour to the data it uses.
notes.analogy: A single office clerk who handles hiring, payroll and the coffee machine: every request queues at one desk.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: God Object vs Big Ball of Mud?
notes.back: God Object: one class hoards responsibilities. Big Ball of Mud: a whole system with no discernible structure. The first is fixed by extraction, the second by drawing boundaries.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: Foote and Yoder: why is the Big Ball of Mud so common, and what's the concrete way out?
notes.back: It works and is cheap at first: throwaway code that stays, piecemeal growth, deadline pressure. Out: carve one boundary at a time and strangle old parts behind it.
notes.source: Foote & Yoder · Big Ball of Mud

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: Every new requirement becomes a Kafka topic, or every problem a stored procedure. Name the anti-pattern?
notes.back: Golden Hammer: a familiar tool applied to everything because it worked before.
notes.analogy: When all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: Spring's AbstractSingletonProxyFactoryBean is the stock joke for which anti-pattern, and what is the remedy?
notes.back: Pattern-itis: patterns stacked without forces to justify them. Ask 'what varies here?'; inline indirections that have one implementation.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: Order has only getters/setters; OrderService computes totals, applies discounts, changes status. Name and why Fowler objects?
notes.back: Anemic Domain Model: procedural code dressed as objects. You pay the mapping costs of a domain model without its encapsulation.
notes.extra: Remedy: move rules into Order (order.applyDiscount()): tell, don't ask. Honest alternative: for simple create-read-update-delete (CRUD) screens, a plain transaction script.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: A module nobody understands contains functions no one dares delete ('might still be called'). Anti-pattern and remedy?
notes.back: Lava Flow: dead code from past experiments hardened into the system. Remedy: telemetry or coverage to prove it's unused, then delete; version control is the safety net.
notes.analogy: Cooled lava: once fluid, now rock that everything is built on.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: Lava Flow vs Boat Anchor?
notes.back: Lava Flow: once-used code whose purpose is now unknown. Boat Anchor: code kept 'just in case' that never had a real use, e.g. an unused plugin framework.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: OrderProcessingStarter is created, calls processor.run(), and is thrown away. Anti-pattern and fix?
notes.back: Poltergeist: a short-lived class with no state or responsibility of its own. Inline it into the caller.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: A bug is fixed in calcTaxEU() but its pasted twin calcTaxUK() still fails in production. Anti-pattern?
notes.back: Copy-paste programming: duplicated knowledge must be changed in every copy. Extract the shared logic once the copies prove to be the same rule.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: price * 1.19 appears in 30 places. Why is a named constant VAT = 1.19 still not enough?
notes.back: The rate is business knowledge that varies by country and date. Make it a domain concept (TaxPolicy.rateFor(country, date)), not just a name.
notes.extra: Magic number: a literal whose meaning and origin aren't visible where it is used.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: order.status = "shiped" compiles and runs. Anti-pattern and fix?
notes.back: Stringly-typed code, a form of Primitive Obsession. Use an enum or sum type so typos are compile errors and the possible values are listed.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: A team builds a 'configurable' rules engine with tables for conditions, operators and actions. What anti-pattern is this?
notes.back: Inner-platform effect: a poor re-implementation of the platform (a programming language) inside it, without tests, types or debugger.
notes.analogy: Building a worse car inside your car so you can 'drive without a car'.
notes.extra: Cousin: entity–attribute–value (EAV) tables that re-implement a schema.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: A class must be called init(), then configure(), then start(), or it crashes. Anti-pattern and fix?
notes.back: Sequential coupling. Do the setup in the constructor or a builder, or use typestate so only legal next calls exist.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: To understand save() you jump through six levels of inheritance and back. Name and remedy?
notes.back: Yo-yo problem. Flatten the hierarchy and replace inheritance with composition so behaviour is in one or two places.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: Which Gang of Four (GoF) pattern is an Express or ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline?
notes.back: Chain of Responsibility: each handler processes the request and either calls next() or short-circuits (e.g. auth returning 401).
notes.analogy: Airport security lanes: each checkpoint inspects you and either waves you on or sends you back.
notes.extra: Same shape: HTTP client interceptors (OkHttp, Axios), servlet filters.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.text: Java I/O: new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(f))): BufferedReader is a {{c1::Decorator}}, InputStreamReader is an {{c2::Adapter}} (bytes → characters).

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: Spring's JdbcTemplate.query(sql, rowMapper): which pattern?
notes.back: Template Method in callback form: the template owns connection, statement, exceptions and cleanup; you supply only the row mapping.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: Hibernate's lazy-loaded order.getCustomer() throws LazyInitializationException after the session closes. Which pattern is behind it?
notes.back: A virtual Proxy: a stand-in that loads the real object on first access, which fails once its session is gone.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.text: React: the component tree is a {{c1::Composite}}; a higher-order component that wraps another to add behaviour is a {{c2::Decorator}}; a useEffect subscription to a store is an {{c3::Observer}}.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: Why can Redux DevTools 'time-travel' through app states?
notes.back: Actions are plain, serialisable Command objects and reducers are pure, so replaying the action log recreates any past state.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: A Git tree object contains blobs and other trees. Which pattern?
notes.back: Composite: directories and files share one interface (objects by hash), and a tree is made of trees.
notes.extra: Bonus: content addressing stores identical content once, a sharing idea close to Flyweight.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: A Kubernetes controller watches resources and reconciles. What Gang of Four (GoF) pattern does the watch resemble, and what's different?
notes.back: Observer for the notifications, but the reconcile is level-triggered: it re-reads the whole desired and actual state rather than trusting the event's payload.
notes.analogy: A thermostat, not a doorbell: it keeps comparing the room with the setting, whatever woke it up.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: Unix grep | sort | uniq -c: which pattern, and what is its in-code equivalent?
notes.back: Pipes and Filters (an architectural pattern, not Gang of Four). In code: lazy iterator or stream pipelines, filter().map().reduce().

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: Java Database Connectivity (JDBC): your code uses Connection/Statement; Postgres and Oracle ship drivers. Which pattern?
notes.back: Bridge: the API abstraction and the driver implementations vary independently. ServiceLoader discovers drivers as plugins.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: A SQL database executes a plan as a tree of operators (scan, filter, join), each pulling rows with next(). Which patterns?
notes.back: Iterator (the Volcano model: open/next/close) arranged as a Composite tree. Parsing SQL text into that tree is Interpreter-like.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.text: Hidden in everyday code: every for (x : list) uses an {{c1::Iterator}}; list.sort(comparator) takes a {{c2::Strategy}}; addEventListener registers an {{c3::Observer}}.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.front: Simple Logging Facade for Java (SLF4J): which pattern is it, beyond the name?
notes.back: Facade over interchangeable logging back-ends, chosen by what's on the classpath; each binding is an Adapter to Logback, Log4j and others.

notes.deck: Clean Code & Design Patterns::12 Anti-patterns & Patterns in the Wild
notes.text: JUnit: setUp() / test / tearDown() run as a {{c1::Template Method}}; a TestSuite containing tests and other suites is a {{c2::Composite}}.
